checks.question: When formatting a Price or Total column for a UK client spreadsheet, how should you apply the currency formatting?
options: Type a pound sign manually into each cell
Use Currency format (£) with 2 decimal places so calculations still work
Convert the column to Plain Text so zeros stay visible
checks.why: Typing £ manually turns numbers into text and breaks formulas. Currency format keeps values numeric with 2 decimal places.

checks.question: In =IF(D2>=$B$1, "Yes", "No"), why does $B$1 use dollar signs before you copy the formula down?
options: It formats the formula output as US dollars
It locks the target cell row and column (absolute reference) during autofill
It stops Excel from recalculating totals
checks.why: Absolute referencing ($B$1) keeps the threshold cell fixed while D2 updates to D3, D4, and D5 on each row.

checks.question: Before selecting two non-adjacent columns for a bar chart, what must you include and hold down?
options: Select only numbers without headings, holding Shift
Highlight both columns including category headers while holding Ctrl (or Cmd)
Delete all columns between them first
checks.why: Hold Ctrl while selecting non-adjacent ranges and include the column headers so chart axis labels and titles generate cleanly.

dfs-file-hierarchies-search-cloud-backup.title: File Hierarchies, Wildcard Search & Cloud Backups
dfs-file-hierarchies-search-cloud-backup.subject: dfs

checks.question: Which folder and filename structure makes exam evidence easiest for an assessor to verify?
options: Desktop/file1final_NEW2.docx
Project_2026/Invoices/Client Invoice March 2026.pdf
Downloads/scan(4).pdf
checks.why: Logical parent-to-subfolder hierarchies paired with descriptive filenames eliminate confusion and missing-file marks.

checks.question: You need to find every PDF invoice in a busy folder without opening subfolders manually. Which wildcard search works?
options: invoice#pdf
*.pdf
?pdf*
checks.why: The asterisk (*) wildcard matches any characters before .pdf, returning every PDF document inside the searched folder.

checks.question: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule mean in practice?
options: Keep 3 copies of data on 2 different media types, with at least 1 stored off-site or in the cloud
Back up 3 times a year using 2 USB sticks in 1 drawer
Compress files 3 times into 2 folders on 1 laptop
checks.why: Keeping 3 copies across 2 media types with 1 off-site/cloud copy protects against both hardware failure and fire or theft.

checks.question: Which built-in feature best helps a colleague with low vision or dyslexia read a long workplace document cleanly?
options: Reducing screen brightness to minimum
Enabling High Contrast / Display scaling, Screen Reader, or larger sans-serif spacing
Switching the keyboard layout to a different language
checks.why: Display scaling, High Contrast themes, screen readers, and generous sans-serif spacing directly improve visual and reading accessibility.

checks.question: When a workplace printer or video call stops working, what should you check FIRST before reinstalling software?
options: Factory-reset the computer immediately
Check power/cables/Wi-Fi connection and read any exact error message
Buy replacement hardware straight away
checks.why: Systematic troubleshooting starts with physical connections, network status, and reading the exact error message before deeper steps.

checks.question: When adding a chart or photograph to an accessible leaflet, what extra step must you complete for screen-reader users?
options: Add descriptive Alt Text explaining what the image shows
Make the image border thicker
Remove all headings from the page
checks.why: Descriptive Alternative Text (Alt Text) allows screen readers to convey key visual information accurately.

checks.question: An urgent email claims your payroll account will close in 1 hour and shows a masked link from support@pay-check-alert.co. What is the first giveaway?
options: It uses polite greetings
Manufactured urgency paired with a mismatched, unofficial sender domain
It arrives on a weekday morning
checks.why: Phishing attacks combine false urgency or fear with lookalike domains to push you into clicking before checking.

checks.question: Which password strategy gives the strongest everyday protection alongside Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
options: Reusing one 8-character word across all sites
Three random words (a long passphrase) unique to each account plus MFA
Writing your birthday with one capital letter
checks.why: Three random words create high length and entropy while remaining memorable, and MFA blocks logins even if a password leaks.

checks.question: Under UK GDPR, if you collect customer phone numbers for a delivery booking, what are you NOT allowed to do?
options: Store them securely with restricted access
Add everyone to marketing lists or share data without explicit consent and a lawful purpose
Delete records once they are no longer needed
checks.why: UK GDPR requires personal data to be collected only for a clear lawful purpose, kept secure, and never shared or marketed without consent.

checks.question: You are emailing 25 external customers about a venue change and must protect their email addresses from each other. Which field should hold their addresses?
options: To
CC (Carbon Copy)
BCC (Blind Carbon Copy)
checks.why: BCC hides recipients' addresses from everyone else on the email, preventing a personal-data breach.

checks.question: A manager sends a team-wide memo and asks only you to confirm your shift availability. Which button should you click?
options: Reply All so every colleague sees your shift
Reply so only the manager receives your individual response
Forward to an external address
checks.why: Use Reply when your response is only relevant to the sender; reserve Reply All strictly for updates the whole thread needs.

checks.question: Before clicking Send on a workplace email with a PDF attachment, what final check prevents the top exam slip?
options: Check the recipient field, clear subject line, professional sign-off, and confirm the right file is attached
Leave the subject line blank so it looks urgent
Use casual slang and emojis in formal emails
checks.why: Assessors deduct marks for blank subject lines, wrong recipient privacy (CC vs BCC), or forgetting to attach the requested file.

dfs-onscreen-exam-strategy.title: DFS Onscreen Exam Strategy: Part A & Part B
dfs-onscreen-exam-strategy.subject: dfs

checks.question: At the start of the 90-minute DFS Onscreen exam, how should you arrange your screen and files?
options: Keep everything full-screen and guess folder locations at the end
Use split-screen with the brief alongside your work and inspect every provided starter file first
Rename all original starter files before reading the brief
checks.why: Keeping the exam brief visible beside your working window prevents missed sub-bullets and lets you check starter data accurately.

checks.question: A task asks you to save a poster as 'Community Flyer' in PDF format inside the 'Final' folder. What must you match?
options: Any name and .docx format anywhere on the Desktop
The exact spelling, file format (.pdf), and requested destination folder
Only the colour scheme
checks.why: Digital exams mark both your document edits and whether you saved the exact requested filename and file type in the right folder.

checks.question: In the final 5 minutes before submitting your onscreen assessment, what is the smartest check to run?
options: Close every file without saving
Verify every required file is uploaded/attached, saved after final edits, and nothing is left open or blank
Delete your working spreadsheet after copying numbers into Word
checks.why: Unsaved edits, missing uploads, or submitting a shortcut instead of the saved file are the biggest avoidable DFS losses.

checks.question: Which file extension indicates a compressed archive containing multiple files that needs extracting before editing?
options: .xlsx
.zip
.png
checks.why: A .zip archive packages files together; extracting (unzipping) it into a regular folder lets applications open and save files properly.

checks.question: You want a client to read a timetable in cloud storage without accidentally deleting or changing figures. Which permission should you set?
options: Can Edit (Owner)
View Only / Read Only
Public Searchable Edit Link
checks.why: View Only / Read Only permissions protect data integrity while still letting recipients read or download the file.

checks.question: What happens if you try to edit files directly inside a zipped preview window without extracting them first?
options: Your changes may fail to save or stay trapped in temporary files
The file automatically converts to a website
Cloud sync doubles your storage space
checks.why: Always Extract All into a named folder first so edits save cleanly to real files you can upload.

checks.question: When turning plain text into a 1-page event flyer or notice, what establishes clear visual hierarchy immediately?
options: Making every single sentence bold and centred
Consistent heading levels, clear body font size, bullet points, and aligned margins
Using five different novelty script fonts
checks.why: Clear visual hierarchy uses a distinct title, clean subheadings, readable body text, and structured lists rather than cluttered formatting.

checks.question: If an inserted logo pushes your text awkwardly onto separate lines, which setting lets text flow neatly beside it?
options: Text Wrapping (e.g. Square or Tight)
Spellcheck Language
Page Orientation Lock
checks.why: Applying Square or Tight Text Wrapping lets paragraphs align cleanly beside images while keeping a single-page layout.

checks.question: Before exporting a single-page poster or newsletter as a PDF, what should you inspect in Print Preview?
options: That nothing spills onto a blank page 2, tables fit inside margins, and all headings/footers look balanced
That all text is invisible white
That the footer sits in the middle of the page
checks.why: Print Preview catches 2-line page overflows, clipped tables, and awkward page breaks before you export.

checks.question: What character MUST every Excel or Calc formula start with so the spreadsheet actually calculates it?
options: An equals sign (=)
A pound sign (£)
A hash sign (#)
checks.why: Without a leading equals sign (=), Excel treats SUM(B2:B8) as plain text instead of running a calculation.

checks.question: Which formula correctly calculates the mean of cells C2 through C10?
options: =MEAN(C2:C10)
=AVERAGE(C2:C10)
=SUM(C2+C10)
checks.why: Spreadsheets use =AVERAGE(range) to find the mean; =MEAN is not a valid spreadsheet function name.

checks.question: What common mistake loses marks on spreadsheet bar or pie charts in DFS exams?
options: Including the Total row in the plotted bars/slices or forgetting a descriptive chart title and axis labels
Adding data labels to make values clear
Using Currency format on price totals
checks.why: Plotting the Total row distorts the scale and duplicates data; always exclude totals and add clear titles and axis labels.

checks.question: What notes are you allowed to take into your Speaking, Listening & Communicating presentation?
options: A full word-for-word essay script to read aloud
A concise 1-page prompt sheet or cue cards with bullet points and key facts
No notes or visuals at all
checks.why: Bullet-point cue cards keep you natural, maintain eye contact, and avoid sounding like you are reading a memorised script.

checks.question: To pass Level 2 SLC, what must you demonstrate in BOTH the presentation Q&A and the group discussion?
options: Speaking for as long as possible without letting others talk
Listening actively, answering questions clearly with reasons, and building respectfully on others' points
Agreeing silently with every statement
checks.why: Examiners assess both clear speaking (facts, structure, tone) and active listening (responding relevantly and inviting others in).

checks.question: If your mind goes blank or you get asked a tough follow-up question, what keeps your marks intact?
options: Say 'I don't know' and stop talking
Use a calm recovery phrase ('That's a great point — let me check my notes / looking at the evidence...')
Change the subject to an unrelated topic
checks.why: A composed pause and bridge phrase keeps communication professional and buys time to give a reasoned response.

english-slc-discussion.title: SLC Task 2: Formal Group Discussion & Turn-Taking
english-slc-discussion.subject: slc

checks.question: What does strong balanced collaboration look like at the start of a formal group discussion?
options: Talking non-stop for three minutes before anyone else speaks
Making a clear opening point, then inviting another group member's view with a question
Waiting until the final 20 seconds to speak once
checks.why: Level 2 expects you to both initiate ideas and draw others into a genuine two-way discussion.

checks.question: Which phrase best shows polite disagreement while advancing the group towards a decision?
options: 'That idea makes no sense at all.'
'I see why flexible hours help, however have we considered how peak shift cover would work?'
'Whatever you say is fine.'
checks.why: Acknowledging the other person's point before raising a reasoned counter-point shows mature Level 2 register and listening.

checks.question: What common habit stops otherwise fluent speakers from passing SLC Task 2?
options: Interrupting peers or giving one-word 'I agree' answers without explaining why
Summarising agreed actions near the end
Using formal workplace vocabulary
checks.why: Interrupting blocks turn-taking, and bare 'I agree' comments show no evidence of reasoning or probing.

english-slc-presentation.title: SLC Task 1: Delivering a Level 2 Presentation & Q&A
english-slc-presentation.subject: slc

checks.question: Which presentation topic works best for a 5–8 minute Level 2 talk and Q&A?
options: A topic with a clear point of view, 3 logical sections, and concrete facts or workplace examples
A single sentence opinion with no supporting evidence
Reading raw statistics for 5 minutes with no conclusion
checks.why: Clear structure (intro, 3 developed points, conclusion) plus real examples naturally sparks strong audience questions.

checks.question: When an audience member asks a challenging question after your talk, how should you structure your reply?
options: Give a defensive 'No' without explanation
Acknowledge the question, give a direct answer backed by a reason or example, and check they are satisfied
Repeat your entire opening paragraph word for word
checks.why: Developed answers with evidence demonstrate Level 2 subject control and active listening.

checks.question: Why should you avoid reading slides or notes continuously during your presentation?
options: It breaks eye contact, flattens vocal pace, and limits audience engagement
Assessors prefer presentations with zero preparation
Cue cards are banned in Level 2
checks.why: Glancing briefly at bullet cue cards lets you project clearly, vary tone, and connect directly with listeners.

checks.question: Why should you reserve dedicated minutes at the end of BOTH Writing tasks rather than writing right up to the bell?
options: Around 42% of Writing marks come from SPaG (spelling, punctuation, grammar, and clear sentences)
Shorter answers automatically get full marks
Examiners ignore spelling if your ideas are good
checks.why: In Functional Skills Writing, SPaG carries roughly 40–45% of total marks; a calm proofreading sweep rescues easy grade-deciding marks.

checks.question: What does the 3-Sweep Proofreading Routine check in order?
options: 1) Word count only, 2) Font colour, 3) Page numbers
1) Sentence boundaries & punctuation, 2) Homophones & tricky spellings, 3) Verb tense, agreement & format
Read quickly backwards only once
checks.why: Separating proofreading into three focused sweeps catches comma splices, homophone slips, and tense drift far more reliably than a single skim.

checks.question: Which sentence contains a classic comma-splice error that proofreading Sweep 1 should catch?
options: 'The training starts at nine; please bring photo ID.'
'The training starts at nine, please bring photo ID.'
'Because training starts at nine, please bring photo ID.'
checks.why: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by just a comma — replace it with a full stop, semicolon, or conjunction.

checks.question: Which sentence uses the correct homophones for ownership and location?
options: 'There leaving they're coats over their.'
'They're leaving their coats over there.'
'Their leaving there coats over they're.'
checks.why: 'They're' = they are, 'their' = belonging to them, and 'there' = place/position.

checks.question: In British English workplace writing, which spelling is correct for the verb meaning 'to rehearse or carry out'?
options: 'We must practice safe lifting before we practise the routine.'
'Staff must practise the fire drill, and this is standard practice.'
'Staff must practice the fire drill, and this is standard practise.'
checks.why: In UK English, 'practise' (with an s, like advise) is the verb, while 'practice' (with a c, like advice) is the noun.

checks.question: Which group of commonly tested Level 2 words is spelled 100% accurately?
options: accomodation, enviroment, definately, seperate
accommodation, environment, definitely, separate
acommodation, environment, definitly, seperate
checks.why: Double c and double m in accommodation, n before m in environment, finite inside definitely, and 'a rat' inside separate.

english-tenses-voice.title: Tense Consistency & Active vs Passive Voice
english-tenses-voice.subject: english

checks.question: Which sentence keeps a consistent past tense throughout?
options: 'Yesterday I visited the centre and speak to the manager.'
'Yesterday I visited the centre and spoke to the manager.'
'Yesterday I visit the centre and will spoke to the manager.'
checks.why: Avoid accidental tense drift ('visited' + 'speak'); keep all verbs in the same time frame unless signalling a deliberate shift.

checks.question: When writing a persuasive complaint email or campaign article, why is Active Voice usually stronger than Passive Voice?
options: Active Voice puts the subject doing the action first, making sentences shorter, clearer, and more direct
Active Voice always avoids naming who is responsible
Passive Voice is banned in formal letters
checks.why: 'Council planners cut three bus routes' (active) is punchier and clearer than 'Three bus routes were cut' — use passive deliberately for formal objectivity.

checks.question: When is switching from past tense to future/modal tense completely valid inside one report?
options: Never — every sentence in a report must stay in one tense
When moving from what happened last quarter (past) to recommended actions (future/should)
Whenever you start a new line mid-sentence
checks.why: Deliberate time shifts (reporting past findings, current status, and future recommendations) are expected in reports; only unmotivated drift is penalised.

checks.question: To hit Level 2 sentence-structure bands, how should you vary your writing?
options: Write only short 4-word simple sentences
Blend simple sentences for impact with compound (FANBOYS) and complex (because/although/when) sentences
Make every paragraph a single 80-word sentence
checks.why: Controlled variety — mixing concise punchy statements with well-punctuated complex clauses — lifts clarity and Band 3–4 composition marks.

checks.question: Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement and formal modal grammar?
options: 'The team of inspectors were late, and they should of called ahead.'
'The team of inspectors was delayed, and they should have called ahead.'
'The list of changes are ready and should of been sent.'
checks.why: 'Team' (and 'list') is a singular collective noun taking 'was/is', and the modal verb is always 'should have' (never 'should of').

checks.question: Where does the comma go when you start a sentence with a fronted subordinate clause: 'Although traffic increased the bus arrived on time'?
options: Right after 'increased,' to separate the fronted clause from the main clause
Right after 'Although,'
No comma is ever used with complex sentences
checks.why: When a subordinate clause leads the sentence ('Although traffic increased,'), place a comma right after it before the main clause.

checks.question: What does the TiPToP rule tell you about starting a new paragraph?
options: Start a new paragraph whenever you change Time, Place, Topic, or Person
Start a new paragraph on every single sentence
Never use more than two paragraphs in an exam
checks.why: TiPToP (Time, Place, Topic, Person) keeps each paragraph focused on one clear idea instead of an intimidating wall of text.

checks.question: In a PEEL body paragraph, what links your paragraphs smoothly for the reader?
options: Discourse markers such as 'Furthermore,', 'However,', and 'Consequently,'
Repeating the exact same opening noun in every sentence
Adding exclamation marks after every line
checks.why: Cohesive discourse markers signal whether your next point builds on, contrasts with, or results from the previous paragraph.

checks.question: Why should a formal email or article avoid a single 25-line block of text?
options: Organisational structure marks require clear paragraphing, topic sentences, and logical flow
It uses too much ink when printed
Examiners only read the first sentence of the page
checks.why: Lack of paragraphing caps Composition & Organisation marks regardless of vocabulary quality.

checks.question: Which structural layout features belong in a Formal Report?
options: Dear Sir/Madam and Yours faithfully
Clear main title, section subheadings (Introduction, Findings, Recommendations), and objective bullet points
A chatty greeting and star rating out of 5 only
checks.why: A Formal Report requires a clear title and logical subheadings leading to actionable recommendations.

checks.question: How does a Balanced Review differ in tone from a Formal Report?
options: A review weighs specific pros and cons for an audience before giving a clear verdict, whereas a report stays formal and objective
A review has no paragraphs or verdict
A report uses slang and personal anecdotes
checks.why: Reviews engage the target audience directly while balancing strengths, drawbacks, and a clear recommendation.

checks.question: What common mistake turns a Report into an Email in Level 2 Writing exams?
options: Adding 'To:/From:/Subject:' headers and signing off with 'Kind regards'
Using formal factual evidence in the Findings section
Including numbered recommendations
checks.why: Do not paste email headers or letter greetings onto a Report; stick strictly to Title + Subheadings + Recommendations.

checks.question: Which opening trio immediately signals an authentic Article or Blog format?
options: Sender address, date, and 'Dear Editor'
An engaging Headline, optional Strapline/Byline, and a lively Opening Hook
'To: All Staff' and 'Subject:'
checks.why: Articles and blogs need a punchy headline, optional byline/strapline, and an opening hook that draws readers straight in.

checks.question: How should the body of a Level 2 article or blog be organised?
options: One unheaded wall of text from top to bottom
Thematic subheadings guiding clear paragraphs with rhetorical questions, facts, and direct reader engagement
Bullet-point notes without full sentences
checks.why: Thematic subheadings plus a persuasive, audience-aware voice (rhetorical questions, rule of three, real-life examples) score top format and style marks.

checks.question: What makes a blog ending feel incomplete or off-format?
options: Closing with 'Yours sincerely' instead of a memorable call-to-action or thought-provoking sign-off
Ending with a direct question for readers
Summarising the main takeaway
checks.why: Never use letter sign-offs ('Yours sincerely') on an article or blog; close with a punchy call to action or lasting takeaway.

checks.question: What makes an effective Subject line in a formal workplace email?
options: 'Hi' or leaving it blank
A concise, specific summary (e.g. 'Staff Rota Update: Bank Holiday Cover')
Writing your entire message inside the Subject box
checks.why: A clear, specific Subject line lets the recipient identify the purpose immediately before opening the email.

checks.question: Which closing matches a formal workplace email addressed to 'Dear Ms Patel,'?
options: 'Cheers, mate'
'Kind regards,' or 'Yours sincerely,' followed by your full name and role
'Love from...'
checks.why: 'Kind regards,' or 'Best regards,' keeps a professional workplace tone cleanly aligned with a named recipient.

checks.question: When writing a complaint or escalation email to a manager, what tone error costs marks?
options: Using aggressive CAPS LOCK, sarcasm, or text-speak instead of calm factual evidence and polite requests
Stating exact dates and times of an incident
Asking for a clear resolution within 7 days
checks.why: Level 2 rewards polite firmness backed by facts; angry outbursts or text-speak breach audience and register criteria.

checks.question: What belongs in the top half of a properly laid-out Formal Letter?
options: Subject line and CC box
Your address (right), Recipient name/address (left), Date, and formal Salutation
Only your first name and postcode
checks.why: Standard UK formal letter conventions require both addresses, the date, and an appropriate formal greeting before Paragraph 1.

checks.question: If you start a formal letter with 'Dear Sir or Madam,', which sign-off MUST you pair with it?
options: 'Yours sincerely,'
'Yours faithfully,'
'See you soon,'
checks.why: Memory trick: 'S' never goes with 'S' — Dear Sir/Madam pairs with Yours faithfully; Dear Mr/Ms [Name] pairs with Yours sincerely.

checks.question: In Paragraph 1 of a formal letter, what should the opening sentence achieve?
options: State clearly why you are writing in the very first sentence
Ask 'How are you doing today?'
Save your reason for the final paragraph
checks.why: Formal letters open immediately with purpose ('I am writing to express concern regarding...') before developing detail and action.

english-planning-paf-audience.title: Planning Your Answer: Audience, Purpose & Context
english-planning-paf-audience.subject: english

checks.question: Before writing Paragraph 1, what does the PAF checklist stand for?
options: Purpose, Audience, Format
Punctuation, Adjectives, Fonts
Paragraphs, Answers, Footnotes
checks.why: Checking Purpose (why), Audience (who), and Format (what text type) locks in the right tone and layout before you write a word.

checks.question: Why should you tick off every bullet point inside the exam prompt as you plan?
options: Missing even one required bullet caps your Task Achievement / Content marks
You only need to answer one bullet of your choice
Bullet points are optional decoration
checks.why: Examiners mark directly against the prompt bullets; turning each bullet into a planned paragraph guarantees complete coverage.

checks.question: If the prompt asks you to write for 'local teenagers' in a youth newsletter, what register mistake hurts your score?
options: Writing in stiff legal jargon suited for a bank director instead of an engaging, accessible voice
Organising ideas into paragraphs
Checking spelling carefully
checks.why: Register must match the Audience — friendly and engaging for peers, formal and respectful for councils or employers.

checks.question: Why should you read the exam questions BEFORE reading every source text word for word?
options: So you skim and scan purposefully for the exact facts, features, and texts each question targets
So you can guess answers without reading the texts
Because reading questions saves you from reading Text C
checks.why: Previewing the questions turns reading into targeted detective work instead of wasting time memorising irrelevant details.

checks.question: When a Level 2 Reading question asks you to 'Explain in your own words...', what loses marks?
options: Lifting and copying an entire sentence verbatim with no rewording
Paraphrasing the core idea accurately and concisely
Checking which text the question specifies
checks.why: Questions requiring 'your own words' penalise copy-pasting; translate the meaning cleanly unless the prompt asks for a direct quote.

checks.question: When a question says 'Using Text B, give two reasons...', what common error earns zero for an otherwise true fact?
options: Pulling the detail from Text A or general life knowledge instead of Text B
Writing two separate bullet points
Checking the wording carefully
checks.why: Always double-check which source letter (Text A, B, or C) a question names — outside knowledge never scores in Reading exams.

english-point-of-view-argument.title: Point of View & Line of Argument
english-point-of-view-argument.subject: english

checks.question: When identifying a writer's 'Line of Argument', what two elements must you trace?
options: Their font choice and word count
Their overall stance (for/against/balanced) AND the step-by-step reasons/evidence they build
Only the final sentence of the article
checks.why: Point of view is the writer's position; line of argument is how they sequence reasons, evidence, and counter-arguments to justify it.

checks.question: Why are signpost connectives like 'However', 'Admittedly', and 'Therefore' vital when answering argument questions?
options: They signal where the writer introduces a concession, shifts direction, or delivers their conclusion
They always indicate a factual table
They prove the writer has no clear view
checks.why: Connectives reveal the logical structure of an argument, separating counter-claims the writer acknowledges from what they actually endorse.

checks.question: A writer quotes a critic's view in Paragraph 2, then writes 'Yet the data proves otherwise' in Paragraph 3. What trap must you avoid?
options: Mistaking the critic's quote for the writer's own viewpoint
Noting both the counter-claim and the writer's rebuttal
Citing paragraph evidence
checks.why: Always check whether the writer is quoting an opponent in order to challenge them rather than stating their own opinion.

checks.question: When asked to identify the writer's 'Tone' at Level 2, which answer is precise enough to earn credit?
options: 'The tone is nice and interesting'
'Skeptical and urgent — shown by warning phrases like "running out of time"'
'It is written in English paragraphs'
checks.why: Vague labels ('good', 'nice') score nothing; name a specific attitude (persuasive, cynical, reassuring, formal) backed by a short word choice.

checks.question: When comparing style between Source A (a council notice) and Source B (a blog), what evidence proves the difference?
options: Contrasting impersonal formal vocabulary and passive constructions against conversational contractions and direct 'you' address
Counting how many pages long each source is
Guessing the author's age
checks.why: Style differences are proved through concrete language choices: formal/impersonal vs chatty/colloquial, contractions, and pronoun use.

checks.question: What common mix-up loses marks on 'Describe the style of Text B' questions?
options: Summarising what Text B is ABOUT (topic) instead of HOW it is written (tone & vocabulary)
Quoting two short phrases to prove the tone
Mentioning formal vs informal register
checks.why: Style questions test HOW the text sounds and addresses readers, not a summary of its topic.

checks.question: Which reliable test separates a Fact from an Opinion in an exam extract?
options: Facts contain statistics or dates, whereas opinions never use numbers
A Fact can be objectively checked and proved true or false; an Opinion expresses a judgement, belief, or value
Facts are always short sentences
checks.why: Even statements with numbers can be opinions ('A disappointing 12% rise'); ask whether the claim is objectively verifiable.

checks.question: Which three clues reveal Bias in a seemingly informative news report or leaflet?
options: One-sided evidence, loaded emotional adjectives, and omitting opposing viewpoints
Using subheadings, dates, and page numbers
Presenting balanced arguments from both sides
checks.why: Bias steers the reader towards one conclusion through selective facts, emotive language, and ignored counter-arguments.

checks.question: Consider: 'The gym opened in 2021 and offers the finest facilities in town.' Why is this a classic Level 2 trap?
options: It blends a verifiable fact ('opened in 2021') with an unverifiable opinion ('finest facilities')
It is 100% factual because it includes a year
It cannot be analysed because it mentions a gym
checks.why: When asked to quote a fact vs an opinion from a mixed sentence, isolate ONLY the exact clause that fits what was asked.

checks.question: Which combination names three valid Language Features (not Layout features) in Level 2 Reading?
options: Bold title, bullet points, text box
Rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language
Subheading, caption, photograph
checks.why: Bold titles, bullet points, and captions are Presentational/Layout features; rhetorical questions, triads, and emotive words are Language features.

checks.question: To gain full credit on a Language Feature question, what does the 3-Part Formula include?
options: Only the technical name (e.g. 'Simile')
1) Name the feature, 2) Short exact quote, 3) Explain its specific effect on the reader in context
Copy out the whole paragraph without naming a device
checks.why: Device + Quote + Context Effect unlocks top marks — generic explanations like 'makes the reader want to read on' score poorly.

checks.question: Which explanation of 'direct address ("you")' earns the explanation mark?
options: 'It grabs the reader's attention.'
'By addressing "you" directly, the writer makes local commuters feel personally responsible for cutting car trips.'
'It uses a pronoun.'
checks.why: Always tie the effect directly to the text's actual topic and target reader rather than using vague stock phrases.

checks.question: Which devices count as Presentational / Organisational Features in a Reading exam?
options: Metaphors and imperatives
Headings, subheadings, bullet points, callout boxes, photographs with captions, and bold key terms
Adverbs and modal verbs
checks.why: Presentational features are visual and structural elements on the page that help readers scan, navigate, and absorb information.

checks.question: How should you explain WHY a writer used bullet points or a callout box?
options: 'To look pretty on the page'
Explain how it breaks dense information into scannable steps or highlights key eligibility/deadline details fast
Copy the text inside the bullet list
checks.why: Link every layout feature to its practical benefit for that reader (e.g. scanning opening hours, contrasting data, or spotlighting warnings).

checks.question: When asked for TWO presentational features used to help readers navigate an article, what trap loses marks?
options: Naming language features like 'rhetorical question' or 'alliteration' instead of visual layout features
Naming subheadings and numbered steps
Mentioning an image and its caption
checks.why: Never confuse Language features (word craft) with Presentational features (page layout, headings, graphics, typography).

checks.question: What is the difference between Explicit and Implicit meaning?
options: Explicit meaning is stated directly on the page; Implicit meaning must be inferred from clues and phrasing
Explicit means long; Implicit means short
Implicit meaning only applies to headlines
checks.why: Reading between the lines (implicit) relies on word connotations, tone, and surrounding context clues.

checks.question: If a question asks for the meaning of an unfamiliar specialist word in context, what should you apply?
options: The Synonym Swap Test: read the sentences before and after, then test your replacement word back inside the sentence
Pick the longest word from another paragraph
Ignore the surrounding sentence completely
checks.why: Testing your proposed synonym back into the original sentence verifies both meaning and grammatical fit.

checks.question: When asked 'What does the phrase "a drop in the ocean" imply about the funding?', what loses marks?
options: Explaining it literally as water falling into the sea instead of meaning 'tiny compared to what is needed'
Explaining that the funding is far too small to solve the problem
Using context from the surrounding paragraph
checks.why: Always interpret idioms and figurative phrases figuratively in the context of the writer's argument.

checks.question: Which are the core writer Purposes tested across Functional Skills Reading texts?
options: To inform, persuade, advise/instruct, describe, or entertain/argue
To type, print, and email only
To increase word count
checks.why: Identifying the writer's primary intention (inform vs persuade vs instruct/advise) frames every comprehension answer.

checks.question: A charity webpage explains local homelessness statistics AND urges visitors to volunteer. How do you explain its purpose at Level 2?
options: Mention ONLY that it informs
Identify its dual purpose: to inform readers about the issue in order to persuade them to volunteer
Say the writer is confused
checks.why: Many Level 2 texts have a primary and secondary purpose; linking them ('informs readers in order to persuade them to...') shows nuanced reading.

checks.question: When asked 'What is the main purpose of Text A?', what common mistake scores zero?
options: Retelling the plot or copying the title instead of stating the writer's aim ('To persuade customers to switch...')
Stating the verb ('to persuade' / 'to instruct') plus specific topic and audience
Checking whether Text A includes a call to action
checks.why: Purpose always starts with an infinitive verb of intention ('to inform / persuade / advise / complain about...'), never just the topic.

checks.question: When you need to find a specific opening time, date, or percentage quickly across 3 sources, which technique do you use?
options: Skimming slowly for overall tone
Scanning rapidly for keywords, numbers, capital letters, or subheadings
Re-reading Source A from line 1 every time
checks.why: Skimming grabs the overall gist quickly; scanning targets exact numbers, names, and keywords for fast fact retrieval.

checks.question: On onscreen Reading exams with multiple source tabs, what habit prevents muddling facts between texts?
options: Verify the active tab title and confirm the exact source letter before typing every quote or reference
Only look at Tab 1 for the entire exam
Copy quotes without checking which tab they came from
checks.why: Confirming the active tab/source letter takes one second and eliminates cross-text mix-ups.

checks.question: When asked for the 'Main Idea' of a 4-paragraph article, what should you avoid?
options: Picking one tiny minor example from Paragraph 3 instead of the overarching message connecting the whole text
Synthesising the headline and topic sentences
Checking the opening and conclusion
checks.why: The main idea captures the big picture across the whole text, not a single isolated supporting detail.

checks.question: When are you allowed to place a semicolon (;) between two clauses?
options: Before a single-item noun
Between two closely related independent sentences that could each stand alone
Instead of every comma in a list of three words
checks.why: A semicolon joins two complete, closely linked sentences cleanly — making it an effortless fix for comma splices.

checks.question: Which sentence uses apostrophes and colons with 100% accuracy?
options: 'The team's goal's are clear; three targets, better pay, safer shift's.'
'The centre's priorities are clear: faster feedback, clearer signage, and longer hours.'
'Its important to check it's opening times.'
checks.why: Never put apostrophes on ordinary plurals ('goals', 'shifts'), use 'it's' only for 'it is', and use a colon after a complete clause to introduce a list.

checks.question: Which sentence properly fixes the comma splice in 'The cafe is busy, it needs two extra staff'?
options: 'The cafe is busy; it needs two extra staff.'
'The cafe is busy it needs two extra staff.'
'The cafe is busy: and it needs two extra staff.'
checks.why: Never fuse clauses with nothing (run-on) or just a comma; use a full stop, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction ('so').

checks.question: Which format pairing matches the required opening and layout conventions?
options: Newspaper Article: Dear Sir/Madam + Yours faithfully
Formal Letter: Addresses, Date, Dear Sir/Madam + Yours faithfully
Formal Report: To/From/Subject email fields + Kind regards
checks.why: Matching every text type (Letter, Email, Report, Article, Review, Leaflet, Speech) to its exact structural markers unlocks Format marks immediately.

checks.question: How does a Leaflet differ visually from an Email in your planning?
options: A leaflet uses a catchy title, bold section subheadings, short scannable bullet blocks, and clear contact/call-to-action details
A leaflet opens with 'Dear Committee Members,'
A leaflet never uses subheadings
checks.why: Leaflets prioritise scannable sections, practical Q&As/bullets, and a clear 'Find Out More' block without letter/email salutations.

checks.question: What happens if your essay is well written in good English, but you write a Letter when the task asked for an Article?
options: You lose heavy marks on Purpose, Audience & Format regardless of SPaG accuracy
Nothing — format does not affect marks
Examiners convert letters to articles automatically
checks.why: Format accuracy is explicitly assessed across Level 1 and Level 2 Writing mark schemes; always check the required text type before writing.

checks.question: What must EVERY comparison point in a Level 2 Reading answer include?
options: Only what Text A says
A direct point from BOTH texts linked with a comparative word (e.g. 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast')
Two separate summaries in unrelated boxes with no link
checks.why: Writing about only one text earns zero comparison marks; both texts must be actively compared side by side on the same point.

checks.question: What does the 3-Layer Synthesis structure combine in one comparison paragraph?
options: 1) Shared/contrasting topic point, 2) Evidence/quote from Source A + connective, 3) Contrasting evidence/tone from Source B
Copying both titles word for word
Listing word counts of both passages
checks.why: Stating the comparison point + Text A evidence + connective + Text B evidence hits every band descriptor cleanly.

checks.question: Why is 'Text A is positive and Text B is negative' too weak without supporting detail?
options: Level 2 requires specific ideas, attitudes, or quotes explaining WHAT each writer is positive or negative about
Because both texts must always agree
Because short phrases aren't allowed in comparisons
checks.why: Always anchor broad claims like 'positive vs negative' with concrete ideas or brief quotes from both texts.

checks.question: In Section A (Non-Calculator), you read a multi-step scale or volume/weight problem mixing kg and g (or cm and m). What check protects the accuracy mark?
options: Convert all measurements into ONE matching unit before calculating, and write the unit clearly on the answer line
Multiply mixed units together and guess the final unit
Drop decimal places because calculators aren't allowed
checks.why: Unit mismatches (cm vs m, ml vs l, £ vs p) void accuracy marks even when the mental arithmetic is right.

checks.question: After dividing a non-calculator quantity in Section A, you get 14 remainder 3 (or 14.3) when packing people into minibuses or boxes. What is the right rounding direction?
options: Round DOWN to 14
Round UP to 15 so the remaining 3 people/items are included
Leave as 14.3 on a bus count
checks.why: Real-life capacity constraints (vehicles, tins, flooring packs) require rounding UP so nobody/nothing is left short.

checks.question: When a Section A question ends with 'Is Samir correct? Show why you think this', what earns the final interpretation mark?
options: Writing only your calculated number without Yes or No
Writing an explicit Yes or No verdict PLUS comparing both calculated figures with units
Writing 'Yes' with zero working
checks.why: Decision marks require BOTH the clear Yes/No conclusion AND the explicit numerical comparison proving it.

checks.question: A question asks: 'Use a reverse calculation to check your answer' (e.g. after 48 × 15 = 720 or 3/5 of 450 = 270). What earns the check mark?
options: Repeating 48 × 15 again
Performing the true inverse step (e.g. 720 ÷ 15 = 48, or 270 ÷ 3 × 5 = 450)
Rounding 720 to 700
checks.why: Repeating the same forward calculation scores zero for a check — use the opposite operation (÷ to check ×, + to check −).

checks.question: Marta thinks she will pay less than £400 of the £720 rent (ratio 9 : 7). How do you lock in the final decision mark after finding £405?
options: Write '£405' alone in the answer box
Tick 'No' AND write '£405 is £5 more than £400' (clear verdict + comparison)
Write 'Yes' because 9 parts > 7 parts
checks.why: Decision questions require BOTH an explicit Yes/No verdict AND a numerical comparison showing £405 > £400.

checks.question: 'One customer who bought a Mini phone is picked at random.' What goes in the denominator of this probability?
options: 50 (the grand total of all customers)
18 (ONLY the Mini phone row/column subtotal — 7/18)
7 (only the 128 GB Mini customers)
checks.why: Conditional wording ('who bought a Mini phone') restricts the denominator strictly to the Mini subtotal (18), not 50.

checks.question: Emma needs flower garland around 2 straight 2 m edges plus two 2.8 m semicircles, and has 40 feet (1 m = 3.3 ft). What two mistakes lose easy marks?
options: Leaving total perimeter in metres (12.792 m) without converting to feet (42.21 ft), OR omitting 'No' when 42.21 ft > 40 ft
Joining the two semicircles into one full circle
Using π ≈ 3.14 × 2.8
checks.why: Always convert into the unit you are comparing (42.21 ft vs 40 ft) AND write an explicit No comparison.

checks.question: Jake's sorted times put 59 and 62 in the middle, giving median 60.5 mins. Which Part (b) check uses multiplication as requested?
options: 60.5 × 2 = 121, and 121 − 59 = 62 (matching the second middle value)
checks.why: When Part (b) specifies a method ('using multiplication'), show the exact inverse step: 60.5 × 2 = 121.

checks.question: In Part (c), 'What percentage of students who revised for MORE than 15 hours scored over 70?' Which students belong in the denominator?
options: All 31 students on the scatter diagram
ONLY the 11 students strictly to the right of 15 hours (8/11 × 100 = 72.7%)
Only students scoring exactly 70
checks.why: Filter to the condition FIRST ('more than 15 hours' = 11 students, NOT counting points sitting right on 15!), then find 8/11.

checks.question: Alya uses 400 kg of flour in April and increases by 14% in May (400 × 1.14 = 456 kg). How can you reverse-check 456 kg on your calculator?
options: 456 ÷ 1.14 = 400 kg (matches April's flour!)
checks.why: To undo a ×1.14 multiplier increase, divide by 1.14 (never multiply by 0.86, which takes 14% of the larger May figure).

checks.question: Karim's tank holds 62 litres (1 gallon = 4.546 litres). Should you multiply or divide 62 by 4.546, and how do you round 13.63836?
options: Divide 62 ÷ 4.546 = 13.638... → 13.64 gallons to 2 d.p. (gallons are larger than litres, so fewer gallons!)
Multiply 62 × 4.546
Round down to 13.63 gallons
checks.why: 1 gallon > 1 litre, so 62 litres equals FEWER gallons (divide!). Watch the 3rd decimal digit 8 rounding .638 up to 13.64.

checks.question: Amir needs 7.9 ÷ 0.215 = 36.74 bricks along the length and 8.6 ÷ 0.065 = 132.3 bricks across. How MUST both counts be rounded?
options: Round UP to whole bricks (37 and 133) before multiplying by 9 bricks high — never buy half-bricks or round 132.3 down!
Round 132.3 down to 132
Multiply 36.74 × 132.3 × 9 and round at the end
checks.why: Every edge needs whole bricks covering the full dimension: 36.74 → 37 and 132.3 → 133; rounding 132.3 down leaves the wall short!

checks.question: 5 bricklayers finish 450 bricks in 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 hours. If a follow-up asks for minutes or checks the time, what does 1.2 hours mean?
options: 1 hour 20 minutes
1 hour 12 minutes (0.2 × 60 = 12 mins — leave as 1.2 when the answer box says 'hours')
2 hours 5 minutes
checks.why: Check the answer-box unit! Writing 1.2 matches 'hours', while converting to minutes multiplies 0.2 × 60 = 12 mins (never 20 mins).

checks.question: In Part (a), how must (13.608 ÷ 3.24)² be entered into a calculator?
options: Type 13.608 ÷ 3.24² without brackets
Divide 13.608 ÷ 3.24 (= 4.2) FIRST inside brackets, then square 4.2 (= 17.64)
Square 13.608 first, then divide by 3.24
checks.why: Without brackets, calculators apply BIDMAS and square ONLY 3.24; always evaluate inside the brackets first.

checks.question: The pool holds 510 m³ and two pumps clear 523.8 m³ in 9 hours. Which answer secures Ben's decision mark?
options: Write '523.8 m³' with no Yes/No
Write 'Yes — 523.8 m³ > 510 m³ (they clear more than the pool volume in 9 hours)'
Write 'No, 523.8 is larger'
checks.why: Notice bigger pump output (523.8 m³ > 510 m³) means YES they CAN empty it in under 9 hours — state Yes + both m³ values!

checks.question: August's estimated mean is 13.24 visits (a 16% increase on July: 13.24 ÷ 1.16 = 11.41). How does Part (b) check the estimated mean 662 ÷ 50 = 13.24?
options: Multiply 13.24 × 50 = 662 (matching the exact sum of Frequency × Midpoint)
Multiply 11.41 × 16
Divide 50 ÷ 13.24

checks.question: In Section B (Calculator), a tank or garden question gives dimensions in m and asks for Litres (or gives Diameter instead of Radius). What MUST you check?
options: Halve diameter to radius for πr², and convert 1 m³ = 1,000 litres (or 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre)
Use diameter directly in πr²
Multiply m³ by 100 for litres

checks.question: When comparing two percentage offers, utility quotes, or mean/range values in Section B, how do you secure the final mark?
options: Stop as soon as your calculator shows the first number
Tick/write Yes or No explicitly AND state both compared numbers with correct units (£, mins, m²)
Round money to £24.3 instead of £24.30

checks.question: Your calculator reads 18.14 tins of paint (or 18.14 m² tiles) needed for a wall, while another question asks how many full £12 tickets £220 can buy (18.33). How do they differ?

Materials covering an area round UP (19 tins), while items limited by a fixed budget round DOWN (18 tickets)

Divide the frequency by the number of table rows

checks.question: Mandy spins a spinner twice and lists every outcome in a sample space. What common mistake costs marks in 'at least one' probability questions?
options: Double-counting the overlap outcome (e.g. Pink + Pink) or forgetting the total outcomes is 5 × 5 = 25
Writing the probability as a simplified fraction
Listing pairs in a systematic 5 × 5 grid
checks.why: A 5 × 5 sample space has 25 equal pairs; count each matching cell once (never add row + column and double-count Pink/Pink!).

checks.question: Habiba mixes butter and flour in ratio 4 : 9 using 650 g total. After finding 1 part = 50 g and butter = 200 g, how do you verify your ratio split?
options: Check flour = 9 × 50 = 450 g, and confirm 200 g + 450 g = 650 g
Multiply 200 × 9
checks.why: Checking both shares add back to 650 g (200 + 450 = 650) guarantees you divided by 4 + 9 = 13 parts accurately.

checks.question: An ingredients list makes 12 cupcakes, and Habiba needs enough mixture for a larger batch. If she scales ingredients cleanly, what check stops under-baking?
options: Scale EVERY ingredient by the same exact multiplier (desired ÷ 12) and round UP whole packs/eggs if needed
Only scale flour and leave sugar at the 12-cupcake amount
Round eggs down when a recipe needs 4.5 eggs
checks.why: Scale every ingredient proportionally, and round UP whole items (eggs, packs) so you never fall short.

checks.question: Callum plots advert spend (0–350) vs enquiries (0–25) on a scatter diagram. When estimating enquiries for an advert spend inside the range, what must you draw?
options: A ruled Line of Best Fit through the cluster, plus vertical/horizontal reading lines to the axis
Only read the highest single dot
Extend the line backwards past zero
checks.why: Examiners award method marks specifically for drawing a straight Line of Best Fit and reading cleanly off the graph grid.

checks.question: Misha weighs 73.3 kg (BMI 25.31), bringing the 8-person team BMI total to 210.41 and mean 26.30 vs target 26.9. What finishes the answer?
options: Write '26.30' alone
State an explicit Yes/No verdict comparing 26.30 against 26.9 with clear reasoning
Divide 210.41 by 7 people instead of 8
checks.why: Always include all 8 team members (210.41 ÷ 8 = 26.30) AND write the Yes/No comparison sentence against 26.9.

checks.question: In Part (a), 'Write three million, six hundred and seventy-five thousand in figures.' Which placeholder mistake loses the mark?
options: Writing 3,675,000 cleanly
Dropping the final three zeros (3,675) or misplacing commas
Using spaces every three digits (3 675 000)
checks.why: Three million sits in the 7th digit place (X,XXX,XXX) — count digits from right to left to keep all three trailing zeros in 3,675,000.

checks.question: Nyam sees his screen time fell/rose by a percentage compared to last week. Why is it wrong to find the percentage of THIS week's new figure when working backwards?
options: This week is already the changed amount (e.g. 100% ± %); divide by the decimal multiplier to recover LAST week's 100% original
Last week's time is always 10 hours
Percentages work identically forwards and backwards
checks.why: Reverse percentage problems always divide the new amount by the growth/reduction multiplier (e.g. ÷ 1.20 or ÷ 0.85).

checks.question: Frank's kitchen is 3.6 m × 4.5 m and heated underfloor area is 8.36 m² (Large kit £179.99). Why should Part (b)'s check test a reverse step?
options: Confirming how area minus unheated fixtures gives 8.36 m², and checking any kit sizing covers AT LEAST 8.36 m² (never under-size!)
Choosing a kit covering 8.0 m² because it's cheaper
Using perimeter instead of area
checks.why: Heating/flooring kits must cover AT LEAST the calculated area (8.36 m²), and Part (b) requires a reverse arithmetic check.

checks.question: Sammi's cylindrical sweet tin sits on a 1 cm grid showing DIAMETER = 6 squares (6 cm) and height = 8 cm. What radius goes into V = πr²h?
options: r = 6 cm (using diameter directly)
r = 3 cm (halving the 6 cm diameter → 3.14 × 3² × 8 = 226.08 cm³)
r = 8 cm
checks.why: Halve the 6 cm diameter to r = 3 cm before computing πr²h = 226.08 cm³ — using r = 6 makes the tin 4× too huge!

checks.question: Part (a) asks for 15/7 as a mixed number, and Part (b) asks for a Median from a dataset. What step comes BEFORE picking the middle value?
options: Sort all numbers in order from smallest to largest (and convert 15 ÷ 7 = 2 remainder 1 → 2 1/7)
Pick the middle number straight from the unsorted board
Write 15/7 as 1.57
checks.why: Divide top by bottom for mixed numbers (15 ÷ 7 = 2 1/7), and ALWAYS sort data ascending before locating the median.

checks.question: Part (a) converts 28% to a decimal (0.28). In Part (b), when converting currency AND adding a fee, what catches candidates out?
options: Multiplying when they should divide (or adding a % fee in £ instead of the foreign currency, and forgetting 2 d.p. money format)
Writing 28% as 0.28
Keeping 2 decimal places on £
checks.why: Check the direction of the exchange rate (home → foreign vs foreign → home) and keep fees in matching currency before rounding to 2 d.p.

checks.question: Bilal's usual pay is £8.70/h with Sunday uplift, plus a Range comparison for consistency. When comparing two ranges, which dataset is MORE consistent?
options: The dataset with the SMALLER range (smaller gap between highest and lowest)
The dataset with the larger range
The one with more entries
checks.why: Smaller Range = values clustered closer together = MORE consistent! Pair with a clear Yes/No comparison statement.

checks.question: Norbert's 12-hour shift starts Monday 8 pm, followed by 30 hours off. Why should you split 30 hours into 24 h + 6 h?

Because there are 10 hours in a day
So you subtract 12 hours twice

checks.question: Zac estimates 3/5 of 624 by rounding 624 → 600 (600 ÷ 5 × 3 = 360). How does Part (b) show a valid reverse check?

checks.question: In Part (a) Company A made 'three quarters of a million pounds' (£750,000), and Part (b) orders 2.39, 2.41, 2.89, 2.9, 3.09. Why is 2.9 LARGER than 2.89?
options: Padding to 2 d.p. turns 2.9 into 2.90, and 2.90 > 2.89
2.9 is smaller because 9 < 89
Three quarters of a million is £75,000
checks.why: Pad decimals mentally to matching places (2.90 vs 2.89) and convert '3/4 of a million' to 750,000 carefully!

checks.question: Alex won 60% of 90 (54) and Seamus won 55% of 80 (44). Alex claims she won 12 more. What goes in the answer box?
options: Write '10' alone
Write 'No, 10 more' (showing 54 − 44 = 10, which is not 12)
Write 'Yes, 54 more'
checks.why: Always pair your explicit 'No' decision with the actual difference (10 more) to win the interpretation mark.

checks.question: Akeem's L-shaped room has area 29.23 m² and each pack covers 0.4 m², giving 29.23 ÷ 0.4 = 73.075 packs. Why does 73.075 round UP to 74?
options: 73 packs only cover 29.20 m², leaving 0.03 m² uncovered — you must buy 74 whole packs
Because .075 is more than .5
You can buy 0.075 of a pack
checks.why: Flooring/tiling/paint packs must ALWAYS round UP even at .075 so the whole room is covered!

checks.question: When plotting 0.7 on a 0-to-1 scale split into 10 equal ticks and measuring the bearing FROM the hostel, what two things check accuracy?
options: Count 7 tenths ticks along from 0, and centre your protractor at the hostel (after FROM) measuring clockwise from North
Count from 1 backwards
Measure anti-clockwise from the cave
checks.why: Bearings ALWAYS measure clockwise from North at the point named after FROM (e.g. from the hostel).

checks.question: When drawing Jesse's 5-year bar chart, what three checklist items secure ALL chart marks?
options: 1) Chart title, 2) Labelled axes with uniform scale starting at 0, 3) Equal-width bars with neat gaps matching table heights
Draw bars touching with no axis labels
Skip the lowest year
