options: Halve diameter to radius for πr², and convert 1 m³ = 1,000 litres (or 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre)
Use diameter directly in πr²
Multiply m³ by 100 for litres
checks.why: Forgetting to halve diameter to radius (4× error) and forgetting 1 m³ = 1,000 litres are the top Section B capacity traps.

checks.question: When comparing two percentage offers, utility quotes, or mean/range values in Section B, how do you secure the final mark?
options: Stop as soon as your calculator shows the first number
Tick/write Yes or No explicitly AND state both compared numbers with correct units (£, mins, m²)
Round money to £24.3 instead of £24.30
checks.why: Examiners look for a stated Yes/No verdict supported by both figures (and 2 decimal places on money like £24.30).

checks.question: Your calculator reads 18.14 tins of paint (or 18.14 m² tiles) needed for a wall, while another question asks how many full £12 tickets £220 can buy (18.33). How do they differ?
options: Both round down to 18
Materials covering an area round UP (19 tins), while items limited by a fixed budget round DOWN (18 tickets)
Both round up to 19
checks.why: Coverage/capacity rounds UP so you finish the job; budget/stock limits round DOWN because you cannot exceed your cash or ribbon!

checks.question: How do you apply a Reverse Check to a Grouped Mean or Reverse Percentage answer in Section B?
options: Multiply Estimated Mean × Total Frequency = ∑(f × mid), OR multiply Original Price × Multiplier back to the given Sale Price
Guess whether the answer looks big
Divide the frequency by the number of table rows
checks.why: Running the inverse calculation confirms both your formula setup and every calculator button press.

checks.question: Before writing 'two million, forty-five thousand and eight' in figures, what stops you dropping a digit?
options: Skip the zero in the hundred-thousands column
Draw place-value columns (M | HTh TTh Th | H T U) and pad empty places with 0 (2,045,008)
Write it as 2,45,008
checks.why: Missing placeholder zeros (writing 245,008 instead of 2,045,008) is the #1 large-number slip; grouped thousands columns prevent it.

checks.question: When dividing 4.8 by 100, which way do the digits shift across the place-value columns?
options: Two columns to the right, giving 0.048
Two columns to the left, giving 480
One column to the right, giving 0.48
checks.why: Dividing by 100 makes a number 100 times smaller — digits shift two places right across the decimal point (4.8 → 0.048).

checks.question: What is the true value of the digit 6 in 3,462,900?
options: 60,000 (sixty thousand)
checks.why: Reading from the right (U, T, H, Th, TTh), the 6 sits in the ten-thousands column, so its value is 60,000.

checks.question: Before ordering 0.4, 0.375, and 0.42 from smallest to largest, what setup step prevents comparing digit length by mistake?
options: Round every number to the nearest whole number
Pad trailing zeros so every decimal has 3 decimal places: 0.400, 0.375, 0.420
Compare only the last digit of each number
checks.why: Zero-padding turns 0.4 into 0.400 so you immediately see 0.375 < 0.400 < 0.420 instead of assuming 375 > 4.

checks.question: Which temperature is COLDER on a number line: -8 °C or -3 °C?
options: -3 °C, because 3 is smaller than 8
-8 °C, because it lies further to the left below zero
They are the same temperature
checks.why: Below zero, larger digits mean further below freezing — -8 °C is 5 degrees colder than -3 °C.

checks.question: Once you finish sorting padded decimals like 0.400, what must you write on the official answer line?
options: Write back the original unpadded forms (0.4) in the exact requested order (smallest-to-largest or largest-to-smallest)
Always write largest to smallest even if the question asks for ascending
Leave out any negative signs
checks.why: Always check the requested direction (ascending vs descending) and copy back the original decimal figures given in the question.

checks.question: When setting up £145.80 − £39 in a vertical column subtraction, how should you write £39?
options: Align 39 on the far right under .80
Pad £39 to £039.00 so every decimal point and place-value column lines up cleanly
Subtract 39 from 80 first
checks.why: Padding whole pounds to £39.00 aligns Units under Units and Tens under Tens so pence are never subtracted from whole pounds.

checks.question: In 500 − 164, where do you borrow (decompose) from when the Units and Tens columns are both 0?
options: Flip the digits and calculate 4 − 0 instead
Borrow 1 hundred from 5 (leaving 4), turn Tens into 10 then 9, giving 10 Units
Turn both zeros into 1s
checks.why: Pass the borrowed value step by step from Hundreds → Tens → Units (4 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 units) — never subtract upwards!

checks.question: After working out 500 − 164 = 336, which reverse check proves your answer is right?
checks.why: Adding your answer (336) back to the subtracted number (164) must reconstruct the starting amount (500).

checks.question: Before multiplying 3.4 × 2.5 by hand, what is the cleanest setup?
options: Multiply 34 × 25 as whole numbers first, counting 2 decimal places total to put back at the end
Drop both decimal points and leave the answer as 850
Round both to 3 × 2 and submit 6 as exact
checks.why: Converting 3.4 × 2.5 into whole numbers (34 × 25 = 850) keeps place value tidy; 2 total decimal digits puts the point back to give 8.50.

checks.question: In long multiplication 47 × 32, what MUST go into the units column on the second row when multiplying by the 3 (30)?
options: Nothing — start straight under the units
A placeholder zero (0) because the 3 stands for 30
A decimal point
checks.why: Forgetting the placeholder 0 on the tens row turns 30 × 47 into 3 × 47 — the classic Non-Calculator multiplication mistake.

checks.question: Estimate 3.4 × 2.5 to check your decimal point placement: 3 × 3 = 9. What does that immediately expose if you wrote 85.0?
options: 85.0 is 10 times too big — the decimal point must sit after 8 (8.5)
85.0 is close enough to 9
You need to multiply by 10 again
checks.why: A quick 1-second rounded estimate catches misplaced decimal points instantly.

checks.question: Which number sits INSIDE the bus-stop shelter in 432 ÷ 6?
options: 6 sits inside and 432 sits outside
432 (the total being shared) sits inside, and 6 (the divisor) sits outside
Either number can go inside
checks.why: In A ÷ B, the first number A (the dividend being shared out) always goes inside the bus stop; B goes outside.

checks.question: A school trip has 124 pupils and each minibus holds 16 seats. 124 ÷ 16 = 7.75. How many minibuses must be booked?
options: 7 minibuses (round down)
8 minibuses (round UP so nobody is left behind)
7.75 minibuses
checks.why: Real-world capacity constraints (buses, paint tins, tiles) require rounding UP so everyone/everything is covered; 7 buses only hold 112.

checks.question: Now flip it: you have £50 to buy £7 notebooks. 50 ÷ 7 = 7.14. What is the maximum number of notebooks you can buy?
options: 8 notebooks
7 notebooks (round DOWN because you cannot afford an 8th)
7.14 notebooks
checks.why: When limited by a budget, ribbon length, or flour stock, any fractional remainder cannot form another full item — round DOWN.

checks.question: In the expression 5 + 3 × 4², which operation MUST be evaluated FIRST?
options: 5 + 3 (reading left to right)
4² (Indices before Multiplication and Addition)
checks.why: BIDMAS executes Brackets → Indices (powers/roots) → Division & Multiplication → Addition & Subtraction.

checks.question: In 24 ÷ 6 × 2, does Multiplication beat Division, or do you work left to right?
options: Work 6 × 2 first because M comes before D in 'DM'
Division and Multiplication share equal rank — work strictly left to right: (24 ÷ 6) × 2 = 8
Either order gives the same answer
checks.why: D/M are equal partners (left-to-right), just as A/S are equal partners (left-to-right): 24 ÷ 6 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8.

checks.question: What does 5² mean on a non-calculator paper?
checks.why: Squaring multiplies the number by itself (5 × 5 = 25), never multiplying by 2!

checks.question: How many rectangular faces (plus 2 square/rectangular ends) does a standard closed cuboid have in its 2D net?
options: 4 faces
6 faces in matching opposite pairs
8 faces
checks.why: Every closed cuboid has 6 faces (top/bottom, front/back, left/right) — missing the lid leaves 5 faces for an open box.

checks.question: What is the 'Plan View' of a 3D building or object?
options: The view looking straight down from directly above (bird's-eye view)
The view from the front door
The diagonal 3D sketch
checks.why: Plan = looking directly down from above; Front Elevation = looking straight at the front; Side Elevation = looking from the side.

checks.question: When folding a net on a grid, what instantly makes two flaps invalid as opposite faces?
options: If two identical flaps fold onto the exact same face (overlapping) leaving another face uncovered
If opposite faces have the same dimensions
If edges are drawn in pencil
checks.why: Mentally fold from the base square: each side edge of an adjacent face must match the edge it meets, with no two faces landing on the same side.

checks.question: What is the sum of interior angles inside ANY triangle vs on a straight line?
options: Both add up to 180°
Triangle = 360°, straight line = 90°
Triangle = 180°, straight line = 360°
checks.why: Angles on a straight line and angles inside any triangle both sum to 180°, while angles around a point or inside a quadrilateral sum to 360°.

checks.question: When using Pythagoras (a² + b² = c²) to find a SHORTER side instead of the hypotenuse, what operation changes?
options: Subtract the shorter square from the hypotenuse square (c² − a²), then take √
Add a² + b² as usual
Forget to take the square root at the end
checks.why: Add squares to find the longest side (hypotenuse opposite 90°); subtract from c² to find a shorter leg, and always take √ last.

checks.question: Your Pythagoras answer for a right-angled ladder's height against a wall comes out LONGER than the ladder itself. What happened?
options: You added c² + a² instead of subtracting — a shorter side must always be less than the hypotenuse
You forgot to multiply by 2
The ladder is vertical
checks.why: The hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right-angled triangle; any leg longer than the hypotenuse flags an immediate add/subtract mix-up.

checks.question: Before finding the area of a triangle or trapezium, which length do you multiply by the base?
options: The slanted side length
The perpendicular height at 90° to the base (and remember ÷ 2 for a triangle!)
The perimeter of the shape
checks.why: Area uses vertical perpendicular height (never a slanted edge), and triangles must be halved: ½ × base × height.

checks.question: A circular patio has a DIAMETER of 6 m. What MUST you do before applying Area = πr²?
options: Halve the diameter to get radius r = 3 m before squaring
Square 6 directly (π × 6²)
Multiply diameter by 2 to get 12 m
checks.why: Area uses RADIUS (π × r²), not diameter; forgetting to halve diameter gives 4 times the true area!

checks.question: One wall edge is given as 450 cm and the other as 2.4 m. What must you do before multiplying for area in m²?
options: Convert 450 cm to 4.5 m first so both lengths are in metres
Multiply 450 × 2.4 straight away
Divide both numbers by 10
checks.why: Never mix cm and m inside an area multiplication; match both dimensions to the same unit first.

averages-and-spread.title: Averages and Spread (Mean, Median, Mode, Range)
averages-and-spread.subject: maths

checks.question: Before picking the Median of a raw list of numbers, what step MUST you perform first?
options: Put every value in ascending order from smallest to largest
Add them all up and divide by the count
Subtract the smallest from the largest
checks.why: Picking the middle number from an unsorted list is the most common Median mistake — always sort first.

checks.question: When estimating the Mean from a grouped frequency table (e.g. 0–10, 10–20), what two numbers do you multiply on each row, and what do you divide by?
options: Multiply Midpoint × Frequency, then divide total by Sum of Frequencies (NOT number of rows!)
Multiply Upper Bound × Frequency, then divide by 4 rows
Add the midpoints and divide by 2
checks.why: Use class Midpoint × Frequency for each row, sum those products, and divide by Total Frequency (total people/items, never the number of table rows).

checks.question: Two runners have the same Mean time, while Runner B has a smaller Range. What does that tell you when comparing consistency?
options: Runner B is MORE consistent because their spread between fastest and slowest is smaller
Runner B is less consistent
Range measures the average score
checks.why: Average (mean/median) measures typical size; Range measures spread/consistency — a SMALLER range means MORE consistent.

checks.question: What four essentials turn a bar chart sketch into full marks on an exam grid?
options: Equal bar widths, equal gaps (for discrete bars), uniform axis scale starting at 0, and clear axis labels + title/key
Touching bars with random axis jumps like 0, 5, 12, 30
No axis numbers needed
checks.why: Examiners deduct marks immediately for non-uniform vertical scales, missing axis labels, or missing keys on dual bar charts.

checks.question: A survey asks 90 customers, and 18 choose Bus. How do you calculate the exact Pie Chart sector angle for Bus?
options: 18° directly
checks.why: A full circle is 360°; divide 360° by total frequency (90) to find degrees per person (4°), then multiply by each group's count.

checks.question: Pie Chart A has 60 people (50% = 30) and Pie Chart B has 200 people (25% = 50). Why can you NOT say the bigger angle always represents more people?
options: Pie charts show proportions, not raw totals — you must multiply each fraction/angle by its own total sample size
A 90° angle always means 90 people
Pie charts cannot compare two groups
checks.why: Angles show shares of each chart's total; 25% of 200 (50 people) beats 50% of 60 (30 people)!

checks.question: What are the three mandatory rules of every compass bearing?
options: Measure from South, anti-clockwise, using 2 digits
Measure FROM North, go CLOCKWISE, and write with 3 digits (e.g. 045°)
Measure from East, go clockwise, round to 10°
checks.why: North (000°) → Clockwise → 3 digits (065°, not 65°) — break any one of the three and the bearing mark is lost.

checks.question: If the question asks for 'the bearing of Town B FROM Town A', where do you place the centre of your protractor?
options: On Town A (the point after the word FROM)
On Town B
Halfway between A and B
checks.why: Always draw your North line and centre your protractor at the location following the word FROM.

checks.question: The bearing of B from A is 070°. How do you find the Back Bearing of A from B without re-measuring?
options: Subtract from 90°
Write 070° again
checks.why: Opposite directions differ by 180° (half a turn): add 180° if the bearing is under 180°, or subtract 180° if it is 180° or more.

checks.question: In the coordinate point (−3, 5), which axis does the first number (−3) describe?
options: Up/down along the y-axis
Left/right along the horizontal x-axis ('along the corridor, then up/down the stairs')
Always positive distance from zero
checks.why: (x, y) always moves horizontally first (negative = left, positive = right) before moving vertically on the y-axis.

checks.question: How do you find the Midpoint between (−2, 4) and (6, 10)?
options: Average the x-values and average the y-values: ((−2+6)÷2, (4+10)÷2) = (2, 7)
Subtract the first from the second
Multiply both coordinates together
checks.why: A midpoint sits halfway between each coordinate pair, which is simply the mean of the x's and the mean of the y's.

checks.question: When translating a shape by vector (+4, −3), what common slip moves it the wrong way?
options: Moving 4 UP and 3 RIGHT instead of 4 RIGHT and 3 DOWN (mixing x and y)
Counting squares from a matching corner vertex
Keeping the shape the same size
checks.why: Top/first number = horizontal (right/left); bottom/second number = vertical (up/down). Check the same matching corner before and after!

checks.question: The rate is £1 = €1.18. When converting £350 INTO Euros (€), which operation do you apply?
options: Multiply 350 × 1.18 (leaving home £ → foreign currency)
Divide 350 ÷ 1.18
Add 1.18 to 350
checks.why: 1 pound buys 1.18 euros, so 350 pounds buys 350 × 1.18 euros. Always multiply leaving £ into a larger foreign rate, and divide coming back to £.

checks.question: When converting leftover €118 BACK into £ at a bureau de change showing 'We Sell €1.16 / We Buy €1.22', which rate applies?
options: Divide €118 by the Buy-Back rate (€1.22) because the bureau is buying your Euros back
Multiply €118 × 1.16
Take the average of both rates
checks.why: Coming back to £ divides by the rate, and the bureau always uses the rate that gives you slightly fewer pounds (dividing by the larger € number).

checks.question: Your calculator shows £214.3 for a currency payout. How must you write money on the answer line?
options: £214.30 (always 2 decimal places for currency)
checks.why: UK currency (£) and Euros (€) always take 2 decimal places — £214.3 means £214.30 (30 pence), never 3 pence!

checks.question: When adding 14.6 + 3.08 + 7, what makes sure the 7 doesn't accidentally add into the hundredths?
options: Line up all decimal points vertically and pad 7 to 7.00 and 14.6 to 14.60
Align the rightmost digits regardless of the decimal point
Drop the zeros inside 3.08
checks.why: Vertical decimal-point alignment with padded zeros guarantees tenths add to tenths and units add to units.

checks.question: How do you divide 4.8 ÷ 0.12 cleanly without a calculator?
options: Multiply BOTH numbers by 100 first so the divisor becomes a whole number: 480 ÷ 12 = 40
Divide 4.8 by 12 and ignore the 0
Only multiply 0.12 by 100 and leave 4.8 unchanged
checks.why: Scale BOTH dividend and divisor by the same power of 10 until the divisor is a whole number — do NOT shift the decimal point back afterwards!

checks.question: True or False: Dividing 18 by 0.5 makes the answer SMALLER than 18.
options: True — dividing always shrinks a number
False — dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes the result LARGER (18 ÷ 0.5 = 36)
It equals 0.9
checks.why: How many 0.5 halves fit inside 18? 36 halves! Dividing by decimals below 1 produces a larger answer.

checks.question: In the Density formula triangle (Mass at the top; Density and Volume at the bottom), how do you find MASS?
options: Mass = Density × Volume
Mass = Density ÷ Volume
Mass = Volume ÷ Density
checks.why: Cover M at the top of the triangle: D and V sit side by side, so Mass = Density × Volume.

checks.question: Density is given as 2.4 g/cm³, while the tank volume is calculated as 0.05 m³. What MUST you convert first?
options: Convert 0.05 m³ into cm³ (multiply by 100³ = 1,000,000 → 50,000 cm³) so the volume units match g/cm³
Multiply 2.4 × 0.05 directly
Multiply 0.05 by 100 only
checks.why: Volume conversions cube the scale factor: 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 cm³! Match density units before multiplying.

checks.question: A crate's calculated mass is 480 kg and the van payload limit is 450 kg. What finishes the answer for full marks?
options: Write '480 kg' only
State an explicit 'No' decision sentence comparing both numbers: 'No, 480 kg exceeds the 450 kg limit by 30 kg'
Write 'Yes, 450 kg'
checks.why: Decision marks require BOTH a clear Yes/No verdict AND the explicit numerical comparison with units.

checks.question: How do you convert ANY fraction like 5/8 into a decimal on a calculator?
options: Divide numerator by denominator: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625
Write 5.8 directly
Divide 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6
checks.why: A fraction line means 'divided by' — always enter top ÷ bottom (5 ÷ 8 = 0.625 = 62.5%).

checks.question: To compare 3/5, 0.58, and 62% cleanly without guessing, what is the best method?
options: Convert all three into the same form (e.g. percentages: 60%, 58%, 62%)
Compare the denominators only
Round every value to the nearest whole number
checks.why: Putting every value into percentages (or 2-digit decimals: 0.60, 0.58, 0.62) makes comparison instant and mistake-proof.

checks.question: What percentage does 0.04 equal?
options: 4% (multiply decimal by 100 → shift 2 places left)
checks.why: To convert decimal → %, multiply by 100 (0.04 × 100 = 4%, whereas 0.40 = 40%).

checks.question: In the catering cost formula C = 45 + 12n, what invisible operation sits between 12 and n?
options: Addition (12 + n)
Multiplication (12 × n) — evaluated BEFORE adding 45
Concatenation (writing 12 beside n)
checks.why: Letters next to numbers mean multiply (12n = 12 × n), and BIDMAS multiplies before adding the fixed £45 fee.

checks.question: When substituting numbers into a multi-step formula like P = 2(l + w), what happens inside the brackets first?
options: Add l + w inside the brackets FIRST, then multiply the total by 2
Multiply only l by 2 and add w once
Divide by 2
checks.why: Brackets execute first: calculate (l + w), then multiply that sum by 2.

checks.question: A formula gives cooking time T = 40m + 20 (in minutes) where m is mass in kg. How do you find m if total time T = 180 minutes?
options: Work backwards using inverse operations: (180 − 20) ÷ 40 = 4 kg
Add 180 + 20 then multiply by 40
Divide 180 by 20 first
checks.why: Undo the last operation first: subtract 20 (160), then divide by 40 to isolate m = 4 kg.

checks.question: Before adding 2/3 + 1/4, what MUST you do to the two fractions?
options: Add tops and bottoms directly (3/7)
Find a common denominator (12ths): 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12
Multiply only the numerators
checks.why: Never add denominators! Convert both fractions to equivalent fractions sharing the same denominator first.

checks.question: How do you convert the mixed number 3 2/5 into an improper fraction?
checks.why: Multiply whole number × denominator, add the numerator (3×5 + 2 = 17), and keep the denominator (5) unchanged.

checks.question: If a question asks for your fraction answer 'in its simplest form' and you get 12/18, what final check completes the mark?
options: Divide top and bottom by their highest common factor (6) to give 2/3
Leave it as 12/18
Invert it to 18/12
checks.why: Always check whether both top and bottom still share a factor (like 2, 3, 5, or 6) when simplest form is requested.

fractions-of-amounts.title: Fractions of Amounts and Reverse Fractions
fractions-of-amounts.subject: maths

checks.question: To find 3/5 of £250 (forward fraction of an amount), what is the correct two-step order?
options: Divide by the bottom (250 ÷ 5 = 50), then multiply by the top (50 × 3 = £150)
Multiply by 5 then divide by 3
Divide 250 by 3
checks.why: Forward fraction rule: Divide by denominator (find 1 unit part), then multiply by numerator.

checks.question: Wait — what if 3/5 of the total cost IS £150, and you need the FULL original total?
options: Flip the steps: divide £150 by the numerator 3 (1 part = £50), then multiply by denominator 5 (= £250)
Calculate 3/5 of £150 (= £90)
Multiply £150 × 3 ÷ 5
checks.why: Reverse fractions tell you what 3 bar-model blocks equal (£150), so divide by 3 first to find 1 block (£50), then × 5 for all 5 blocks!

checks.question: How do you sanity-check your £250 reverse-fraction answer before moving on?
options: Find 3/5 of £250 (250 ÷ 5 × 3 = £150) and confirm it matches the £150 given in the prompt
Check that £250 is smaller than £150
checks.why: The whole original amount must always be larger than the partial fraction, and taking 3/5 of it returns you straight to £150.

checks.question: When filling missing cells in a Two-Way Table, which line should you tackle FIRST?
options: Any row or column that already has all entries except ONE missing box (including the Grand Total row/column)
Guess the middle cell randomly
Leave the Total column blank
checks.why: Look for any line with just one gap: subtract the known entries from that row or column total to unlock neighbouring cells cleanly.

checks.question: 'One customer who bought a Mini item is picked at random.' What number goes in the DENOMINATOR of this probability fraction?
options: Always the Grand Total (e.g. 50)
ONLY the Mini subtotal (the named subgroup you are picking from)
Only the column total for the other category
checks.why: Conditional probability ('of those who chose Mini...') restricts the sample space to that specific row or column total, NOT the grand total!

checks.question: After completing every empty box in a two-way table, what 5-second check guarantees zero arithmetic errors?
options: Check that ALL row totals AND ALL column totals sum cleanly to the same Grand Total
Check only the top row
Leave percentages unrounded
checks.why: Cross-checking both row sums and column sums against the bottom-right Grand Total catches every slip automatically.

checks.question: Without a calculator, how do you build 17.5% of £240 reliably using easy blocks?
options: Find 10% (£24), halve it for 5% (£12), halve again for 2.5% (£6), then add 24 + 12 + 6 = £42
Divide 240 by 17.5
Round 17.5% up to 20% and leave it
checks.why: The 10% → 5% → 2.5% (and 1%) building-block ladder handles every non-calculator percentage safely.

checks.question: To express '18 out of 45 attendees' as a percentage, what calculation gives the exact %?
checks.why: Write part ÷ whole as a fraction (18/45), then multiply by 100 to convert straight into a percentage.

checks.question: On a calculator, which decimal converts 6% correctly (NOT 60%)?
checks.why: 0.6 equals 60%; single-digit percentages always need a placeholder zero after the point (6% = 0.06).

checks.question: Which single decimal multiplier increases a price by 14%, and which reduces it by 15%?
options: Increase: × 1.14  |  Decrease: × 0.85 (100% − 15%)
Increase: × 0.14  |  Decrease: × 0.15
Increase: × 1.14  |  Decrease: × 1.85
checks.why: Start from 100% (1.00): add 14% → 1.14; subtract 15% → 0.85.

checks.question: A jacket costs £68 AFTER a 15% discount. Why can you NOT simply add 15% of £68 back on to find the original price?
options: Because the 15% was taken off the larger original price (100%) — divide £68 by 0.85 (= £80) instead
Because you should subtract 15% again
Because 85% equals £100
checks.why: 15% of £68 is smaller than 15% of £80! Since £68 equals 85% (0.85) of the original price, reverse it by dividing: £68 ÷ 0.85 = £80.

checks.question: Sales rose from £400 to £460. In the Percentage Change formula ((Change ÷ Original) × 100), what sits on the bottom?
options: The Original value (£400): (60 ÷ 400) × 100 = 15%
The New value (£460)
The Difference (£60)
checks.why: Always divide the change by the ORIGINAL starting value — dividing by the new figure is the #1 percentage-change trap.

checks.question: A room needs skirting board around the walls AND vinyl across the floor. Which measurement matches each job?
options: Skirting = Perimeter (metres around outside)  |  Vinyl = Area (square metres covering inside)
Skirting = Area  |  Vinyl = Perimeter
Both use Volume in m³
checks.why: Edges/fencing/edging/skirting = Perimeter (length); flooring/turf/paint coverage = Area (m²).

checks.question: Before splitting an L-shaped floor into rectangles, how do you find any unlabelled inner edge?
options: Subtract the shorter parallel edge from the matching full horizontal or vertical side
Guess the length by eye
Multiply the two outer edges
checks.why: Opposite horizontal edges share the same total width, and opposite vertical edges share the same total height.

checks.question: Flooring packs cover 2.2 m² each and you need 31.4 m². 31.4 ÷ 2.2 = 14.27 packs. How many packs must be ordered?
options: 14 packs (normal nearest rounding)
15 packs (round UP — 14 packs only cover 30.8 m², leaving an uncovered gap)
14.3 packs
checks.why: Even a decimal like .08 or .27 means you need part of an extra pack/tin — always round UP for materials and coverage.

checks.question: When calculating the perimeter of an L-shape, what must you include when adding up around the outside?
options: ONLY the labelled numbers printed on the diagram
ALL 6 outer edges — calculating any unlabelled vertical or horizontal step first
The inner cut line splitting the two rectangles
checks.why: Skipping unlabelled edges leaves out two sides! Trace every single outer edge around the perimeter like walking a fence.

checks.question: You want the perimeter of a standalone D-shaped SEMICIRCLE of diameter 10 m. After calculating ½(π × 10) = 15.7 m, what else must you add?
options: Nothing — 15.7 m is the full perimeter
Add the straight 10 m diameter edge closing the bottom: 15.7 + 10 = 25.7 m
Square the radius
checks.why: ½πd only measures the curved arc! For a closed semicircle shape, remember to add the straight diameter across the base.

checks.question: When fencing a garden with a 1.2 m wide gate gap, what should you check in the wording before buying fence panels?
options: Subtract the 1.2 m gate gap from the total perimeter if no fence goes across the gate
Leave the perimeter in square metres (m²)
Ignore the gate completely
checks.why: Watch out for doors, gates, or walls already bordering a side — subtract gaps you are NOT fencing or skirting.

checks.question: In any probability tree diagram, what must the decimals or fractions on each pair of branches splitting from ONE node add up to?
checks.why: Every set of outcomes branching from a single point is exhaustive, so their probabilities always sum to 1 (e.g. 0.3 and 0.7).

checks.question: How do you compute the probability of two combined events (e.g. 'Late on Monday AND Late on Tuesday')?
options: ADD the branch probabilities together
MULTIPLY along the branches (AND = ×); ADD separate winning paths together (OR = +)
Divide the first branch by the second
checks.why: Walk ALONG a route by multiplying (AND), then ADD together all routes that match the question (OR).

checks.question: A bag holds 3 red and 7 blue counters. One counter is picked and NOT put back. What changes on the second branch?
options: The denominator drops from 10 to 9 (and the chosen colour numerator drops by 1)
All probabilities stay out of 10
The probabilities double
checks.why: Without replacement leaves 9 items in the bag for the second pick — keeping /10 on the second branch is a classic Level 2 trap.

checks.question: When asked to give a numerical probability on a Functional Skills exam, which answer earns ZERO marks?
options: Writing a ratio like '3 : 7' or '3 out of 10' in words instead of a fraction, decimal, or percentage
Writing '0.0' for an impossible event
checks.why: Examiners explicitly reject ratios ('3:7') and '3 out of 10' on probability lines — always write a fraction, decimal, or percentage.

checks.question: The probability a bus is late is 0.15. Out of 200 journeys, how many late buses are EXPECTED?
options: 200 × 0.15 = 30 late buses (multiply trials n × p)
checks.why: Expected frequency = Number of trials (n) × Probability (p). Here 200 × 0.15 = 30.

checks.question: The probability of winning a prize is 0.18. What is the probability of NOT winning?
checks.why: All outcomes total 1, so P(Not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.18 = 0.82.

checks.question: Which scenario is INVERSE proportion rather than direct proportion?
options: Buying more metres of cable costs more money
More workers sharing the same fixed wall finish the job in FEWER hours
Buying twice as many tickets doubles the total cost
checks.why: In Direct proportion both quantities rise together; in Inverse proportion, doubling workers halves the time needed.

checks.question: It takes 3 painters 8 hours to paint a hall. How long would 4 painters take at the same rate?
options: Find total painter-hours first (3 × 8 = 24 hours), then divide by 4 painters = 6 hours
Multiply 8 ÷ 3 × 4 = 10.7 hours
Subtract 1 hour per extra painter = 7 hours
checks.why: Multiply workers × time to get the fixed total effort (24 worker-hours), then divide by the new number of workers (24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours).

checks.question: You calculated 1.2 hours on your calculator for a proportion time question. What is 1.2 hours in hours and minutes?
options: 1 hour 20 minutes
1 hour 12 minutes (0.2 × 60 = 12 minutes)
1 hour 2 minutes
checks.why: 0.2 hours is two-tenths of 60 minutes (0.2 × 60 = 12 mins), NOT 20 minutes!

checks.question: To share £480 in the ratio 5 : 3, what is the very first step?
options: Divide 480 by 5 and 3 separately
Add the parts (5 + 3 = 8 total parts), then divide £480 ÷ 8 = £60 per part
Subtract 5 − 3 = 2
checks.why: When sharing a TOTAL amount, find total parts first (5+3 = 8), divide to get 1 part (£60), then multiply each person's share.

checks.question: Paint is mixed Red : White in the ratio 2 : 5, and you already have 6 litres of RED paint. How much WHITE paint do you need?
options: Divide 6 by 7 total parts
Since 6 litres = Red's 2 parts, 1 part = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 litres, so White = 5 × 3 = 15 litres
Multiply 6 × 5 = 30 litres
checks.why: When given ONE person's/ingredient's amount (not the grand total), divide ONLY by their ratio parts (2), never by the sum (7)!

checks.question: Simplifying a ratio with mixed units like 40 cm : 2 m: what must happen before dividing by common factors?
options: Convert both to the same unit first: 40 cm : 200 cm → divide by 40 → 1 : 5
Simplify 40 : 2 straight to 20 : 1
Write units inside the final ratio
checks.why: Ratios must share identical units before simplifying (40 cm : 200 cm = 1 : 5), and final simplified ratios have no units.

checks.question: A recipe for 12 muffins uses 180 g of flour. To make 30 muffins cleanly, which scaling route avoids awkward rounding?
options: Divide by 12 to find 1 muffin (15 g), then multiply by 30 (= 450 g) — or scale by × 2.5
Add 18 g because 30 − 12 = 18
Double 180 g and add 12
checks.why: Finding the value for 1 item (Unitary Method) or the exact scale factor (30 ÷ 12 = 2.5) scales every ingredient accurately.

checks.question: Shop A sells 400 g coffee for £3.60; Shop B sells 750 g for £6.60. How do you compare value fairly?
options: Pick Shop A because £3.60 is a smaller ticket price
Compare price per identical unit (e.g. per 100 g or per 1 g): A = 90p/100g vs B = 88p/100g → Shop B is better value
Compare 400 ÷ 3.60 without noting which means cheaper
checks.why: Divide Cost ÷ Weight to compare price per gram/100g (LOWER cost per 100 g = better value), or scale both to a common weight like 100 g.

checks.question: When comparing two packs (e.g. £/100 g vs g/£1), what reversal error catches students out?
options: Dividing weight ÷ price (grams per £1) and picking the SMALLER number instead of noticing more grams per £1 is cheaper
Labeling every calculation with £/100 g units
Comparing equal weights
checks.why: Cheaper cost per unit = lower £/g; higher weight per £ = more g/£1. Always label your units so you pick the right direction!

checks.question: Round 0.0486 to 2 SIGNIFICANT FIGURES (2 s.f.) vs 2 DECIMAL PLACES (2 d.p.):
options: 2 d.p. = 0.05  |  2 s.f. = 0.049 (start counting s.f. at the first non-zero digit '4')
Both give 0.05
checks.why: Decimal places count ALL digits after the decimal point; significant figures start counting only at the first non-zero digit.

checks.question: When an exam says 'Estimate the value of (58.7 × 19.4) ÷ 0.48', what must you do BEFORE multiplying?
options: Calculate the exact answer first and then round it
Round every number to 1 significant figure FIRST: (60 × 20) ÷ 0.5 = 1200 ÷ 0.5 = 2400
Round 0.48 down to 0
checks.why: Estimation marks explicitly require rounding each input to 1 significant figure BEFORE computing — never round 0.48 to 0!

checks.question: What happens to trailing zeros when rounding 3,842 to 2 significant figures?
options: Write 38
Keep placeholder zeros so the magnitude stays in thousands: 3,800
Write 38.0
checks.why: 3,842 is nearly four thousand — dropping placeholder zeros and writing 38 destroys its size; pad with zeros to 3,800.

checks.question: A blueprint uses a scale of 1 : 200. What does a 1 cm line on the drawing represent in reality?
options: 200 metres
200 cm (= 2 metres)
20 cm
checks.why: A 1 : n ratio keeps the same unit on both sides: 1 cm on paper = 200 cm in real life = 2 m.

checks.question: A garden path is 12 m long in real life. On a 1 cm = 2 m scale drawing, how long do you draw it?
options: Divide real length by scale: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm (paper is smaller than real life)
Multiply 12 × 2 = 24 cm
Draw 12 squares regardless of scale
checks.why: Paper → Real Life = MULTIPLY by scale; Real Life → Paper = DIVIDE by scale.

checks.question: On a 1 cm grid plan, you need to draw a shed 3 m × 2 m using scale 1 : 100. Why should you check furniture clearance and grid counts carefully?
options: 1 : 100 means 1 cm = 1 m (1 grid square per metre), so draw 3 squares × 2 squares inside any boundary/clearance limits
Draw 300 squares × 200 squares
Scale ratios ignore orientation
checks.why: Always check what 1 grid square equals (1 cm or 0.5 cm!) and verify doors, walkways, or boundary clearance rules in the prompt.

checks.question: When plotting a new cross on a scatter graph for (12 hours revision, 45 marks), which axis do you read first?
options: Horizontal x-axis (12 hours) first, then straight up to 45 on the vertical y-axis
Vertical axis first, then across
Connect all crosses dot-to-dot
checks.why: Read horizontal axis → vertical axis carefully checking the value of every tiny grid square (e.g. each tick = 2 or 5).

checks.question: How must you draw a valid Line of Best Fit to estimate a missing value?
options: Zig-zag through every single cross
Use a ruler to draw ONE straight line following the trend with roughly equal crosses above and below (ignoring clear outliers)
Always force it through (0, 0)
checks.why: A straight ruled line passing cleanly through the heart of the cluster (never forced through 0,0 unless the data actually points there) lets you interpolate reliably.

checks.question: Why does 'negative correlation' (points sloping down left-to-right) NOT mean 'no correlation'?
options: Negative correlation IS a strong relationship: as one variable rises, the other falls; 'no correlation' has scattered points with no trend
Negative correlation means the graph is wrong
Only upward lines show correlation
checks.why: Upward slope = positive correlation; downward slope = negative correlation; random cloud = no correlation.

checks.question: £2,000 is invested for 3 years at 4% interest. What distinguishes COMPOUND interest from SIMPLE interest?
options: Simple adds 4% of £2,000 (£80) every year; Compound earns 4% on the growing balance each year (× 1.04³)
Compound pays less over 3 years
Simple multiplies by 1.04³
checks.why: Compound interest earns 'interest on interest' — use Balance × (1 + r)ⁿ instead of adding the flat Year 1 amount n times.

checks.question: Which multiplier expression finds the total balance after investing £1,500 at 3.5% compound interest for 4 years?
checks.why: 3.5% = 0.035, so the annual growth multiplier is 1 + 0.035 = 1.035 (NOT 1.35, which would be 35%!), raised to the power of 4 years.

checks.question: After computing £2,000 × 1.04³ = £2,249.73, the question asks ONLY: 'How much INTEREST did she earn?' What must you do?
options: Subtract the £2,000 deposit: £2,249.73 − £2,000 = £249.73 interest
Multiply by 3 again
checks.why: Balance × multiplierⁿ gives the FINAL TOTAL BALANCE; subtract the original principal if the prompt asks only for the interest earned!

checks.question: In the Speed-Distance-Time triangle (D on top; S and T on bottom), how do you find TIME?
options: Time = Distance ÷ Speed
Time = Speed × Distance
Time = Speed ÷ Distance
checks.why: Cover T: D sits over S, so Time = Distance ÷ Speed.

checks.question: A journey takes 2 hours 15 minutes at 40 mph. Which number MUST you enter for Time in Distance = Speed × Time?
options: 2.15 hours
2.4 hours
checks.why: There are 60 minutes in an hour, NEVER 100! Divide minutes by 60 (15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 → 2.25 hours) before multiplying.

checks.question: Your calculator says Time = 1.75 hours. What does 1.75 hours equal on a real clock?
options: 1 hour 75 minutes
1 hour 45 minutes (0.75 × 60 = 45 mins)
1 hour 15 minutes
checks.why: Multiply the decimal fraction of an hour by 60 (0.75 × 60 = 45 minutes) when converting back to hours and minutes.

checks.question: How many lines of reflection symmetry does a standard non-square RECTANGLE have?
options: 4 (vertical, horizontal, and both diagonals)
2 (vertical and horizontal only — folding along a rectangle's diagonal does NOT match!)
checks.why: Squares have 4 lines of symmetry, but rectangles only have 2 — paper folded along a rectangle's diagonal misses the corners.

checks.question: What proves whether regular polygons can TESSELLATE (tile flat with zero gaps or overlaps)?
options: The interior angles meeting at a vertex must add up cleanly to 360° (e.g. triangles 60°, squares 90°, hexagons 120°)
Any 5-sided pentagon tiles cleanly
The edges only need to be curved
checks.why: Angles meeting at a point must divide cleanly into 360° — regular pentagons (108°) leave gaps because 360 ÷ 108 isn't whole.

checks.question: A shape looks the same ONLY once in a full 360° turn. What order of rotational symmetry do we write?
options: Order 1 (or 'no rotational symmetry')
Order 0
Order 4
checks.why: Every shape lands back on itself once in a full 360° turn (Order 1); order 2+ means it matches multiple times before 360°.

checks.question: Which operation converts 3.45 kilometres (km) into metres (m), and which converts 450 millilitres (ml) into litres (l)?
options: Both divide by 1,000
checks.why: 'Kilo-' and 'milli-' step by 1,000 (big unit → small unit multiplies; small unit → big unit divides); only 'centi-' steps by 100.

checks.question: You are given 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lbs. How do you convert 11 lbs into kilograms?
options: Divide 11 ÷ 2.2 = 5 kg
Multiply 11 × 2.2 = 24.2 kg
Subtract 2.2 from 11
checks.why: Kilograms are heavier than pounds (fewer kg for the same weight), so divide lbs by 2.2: 11 ÷ 2.2 = 5 kg.

checks.question: True or False: 1 m² equals 100 cm² because 1 m = 100 cm.
options: True — area converts by 100
False — 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10,000 cm²!
1 m² = 1,000 cm²
checks.why: Square units scale in BOTH length and width (100 × 100 = 10,000 cm²), and cubic volume scales three times (1,000,000 cm³).

checks.question: How does the volume of a TRIANGULAR PRISM differ from a CUBOID of the same base, height, and length?
options: Find the triangle cross-section area (½ × b × h) FIRST, then multiply by length
Multiply b × h × l without halving
Multiply πr² × l
checks.why: Every prism has Volume = Cross-Section Area × Length; for a triangular prism, halve the triangle base × height first!

checks.question: You calculate a fish tank's volume as 48,000 cm³. How many LITRES of water does it hold?
options: Divide by 1,000 → 48 litres (1 litre = 1,000 cm³)
Divide by 100 → 480 litres
Multiply by 1,000
checks.why: Memorise both capacity facts: 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre, and 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

checks.question: A tank is 1.5 m deep, and the prompt warns 'Leave a 20 cm air gap at the top'. What height do you multiply by?
options: 1.5 − 0.20 = 1.30 m water depth (convert 20 cm to 0.20 m first!)
checks.why: Always check for air-gap/fill-line instructions AND convert cm gaps into metres before subtracting.

checks.question: A manufacturer needs to know how much cardboard wraps the OUTSIDE of a closed box. Should they calculate Volume or Surface Area?
options: Surface Area (sum of all 6 outer rectangular faces, in cm² or m²)
Volume (length × width × height, in cm³)
Perimeter
checks.why: Wrapping, painting, or cardboard needed = Surface Area (sum of outer 2D faces); liquid/space inside = Volume.

checks.question: For a cylinder of diameter 10 cm and height 12 cm, which step calculates Volume = πr²h?
options: π × 5² × 12 (halve diameter 10 → radius 5 cm first!)
checks.why: Use radius r = 5 cm (not diameter 10) inside πr²h for volume; 2πrh only finds the curved wrapper label area.

checks.question: When painting the outside of an OPEN-TOP storage tank (no lid), how many faces go into the Surface Area?
options: 5 faces (base + 4 walls — skip the top lid!)
All 6 faces including the missing lid
Only 4 walls
checks.why: Always read whether a box, pool, or tin is open-top (5 faces) or closed (6 faces) before summing areas.

checks.question: In the first 60 seconds of a Level 2 Presentation, what helps the group follow your talk immediately?
options: Giving a clear intro and roadmap stating your topic and the key points you will cover
Reading straight from a long paragraph without pausing
Skipping straight to closing thank-yous
checks.why: Signposting your roadmap early lets assessors tick clarity and logical sequencing criteria right away.

checks.question: When chairing the Q&A after your talk, how does a Level 2 speaker handle a tough or emotional question?
options: Stay calm, acknowledge the speaker's point, and answer with clear policy/evidence-backed solutions
Cut the questioner off and change topic
Reply with 'Yes' or 'No' only
checks.why: Developed answers linking practical solutions back to workplace policy demonstrate strong Level 2 communication.

checks.question: Why does the presenter invite specific peers by name and summarise key points before closing Q&A?
options: It shows active leadership, keeps everyone included, and brings the session to a polished formal close
It fills extra silence without adding points
Examiners penalise summaries
checks.why: Inviting contributions and wrapping up clearly earns top Speaking & Listening interaction marks.

checks.question: How does a strong participant open Task 2 (Group Discussion) cleanly?
options: Frame the shared workplace problem concisely and invite another member's perspective
Talk silently for 30 seconds
Vote immediately without hearing anyone else
checks.why: Framing the issue clearly sets a focused, collaborative agenda for the entire group.

checks.question: Watch how Thomas, Amara, and Constantin interact: what moves the discussion forward toward Level 2 pass marks?
options: Each person builds on the previous point with new workplace evidence (e.g. shift cover or fatigue) instead of repeating the same sentence
Everyone speaks over each other at once
Everyone stays silent except one leader
checks.why: Active listening shows when you refer to what a peer just raised and add practical evidence or a counter-consideration.

checks.question: Before the discussion wraps up, what turns individual ideas into a successful Level 2 group conclusion?
options: Reaching and stating a clear, balanced consensus that addresses everyone's raised concerns
Stopping mid-sentence when the timer finishes
Arguing over an unrelated topic
checks.why: Synthesising a clear consensus or agreed compromise proves collaborative problem-solving across the group.

checks.question: In the sequence 7, 13, 19, 25, ..., how do you find the next two terms cleanly?
options: Check the step gap between consecutive terms (+6 each time) → 31, 37
Double the last term
Add the first two terms together
checks.why: Testing consecutive differences (term-to-term rule) immediately reveals steady arithmetic steps (+6) or descending steps (−4).

checks.question: In 14, [ ? ], 28, 35, how do you verify a missing middle number reliably?
options: Check the step between adjacent known terms (35 − 28 = +7), test 14 + 7 = 21, and verify 21 + 7 = 28
Take any odd number between 14 and 28
checks.why: Confirm the step forward AND backward across your gap — if two gaps span 14 to 28, divide the span by 2 steps (14 ÷ 2 = +7).

checks.question: For a descending temperature sequence like 5, 2, −1, −4, what is the next term?
options: −7 (subtract 3 more past −4)
checks.why: Subtracting 3 moves further left below zero: −4 − 3 = −7.

checks.question: A dial shows 0 and 100 with 5 equal intervals (gaps) between them. What does ONE small tick mark equal?
options: 1 unit
20 units (100 ÷ 5 gaps = 20 per tick)
25 units
checks.why: Never assume 1 tick = 1! Count the number of GAPS between labelled numbers and divide the span by the gap count.

checks.question: On a bus timetable, if the 09:42 bus takes 35 minutes, what time does it arrive (avoiding the 100-minute trap)?
options: 10:17 (18 mins takes you to 10:00, leaving 17 mins → 10:17)
checks.why: Bridge to the next whole hour first (09:42 + 18 mins = 10:00), then add the remaining 17 minutes (= 10:17).

checks.question: Freezer thermometer shows −18 °C and warms to −4 °C. How many degrees did it rise?
options: 14 °C warmer
14 °C colder
checks.why: Moving from −18 up to −4 is an increase of +14 °C (towards 0), not subtracting past zero.

checks.question: How should tallies be grouped so counts stay accurate during an exam?
options: Write tallies in single ungrouped strokes across the page
Cross every 5th mark diagonally across 4 vertical lines (gates of 5) and write the numerical Frequency total beside it
Write only words
checks.why: 5-bar gates prevent counting errors, and always total up your frequency column to match the original item count!

checks.question: Why are Line Graphs used instead of bar charts for monthly rainfall or hourly temperature?
options: Line graphs show continuous change and trends over TIME
Line graphs are only for colours or flavours
Line graphs do not need axes
checks.why: Continuous data over time uses plotted points joined by straight lines to reveal rising, falling, or peak trends.

checks.question: When tallying 20 survey responses into a frequency table, what 3-second check catches a missed item?
options: Add the Frequency column and verify it sums to 20
Count only the largest row
Skip the last response
checks.why: Summing your Frequency column and checking it equals the total survey count catches skipped or double-counted items immediately.

e3-numbers-to-1000-and-patterns.title: E3 Maths: Numbers up to 1,000 & Patterns
e3-numbers-to-1000-and-patterns.subject: maths

checks.question: In the number 604, what does the 0 in the middle stand for?
options: Zero tens — keeping the 6 in the hundreds column (604, not 64)
Sixty tens
Nothing — it can be deleted
checks.why: Zero acts as an essential placeholder in the tens column so 604 stays six hundred and four instead of shrinking to 64.

checks.question: How do you quickly spot whether 738 is odd or even?
options: Look ONLY at the last (units) digit: 8 is even, so 738 is even
Look at the first digit 7
checks.why: Even numbers always end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8; odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9.

checks.question: Count back in steps of 100 from 850: 850, 750, [ ? ], 550.
checks.why: Subtracting 100 changes ONLY the hundreds digit (7 → 6), keeping 50 unchanged to give 650.

checks.question: When setting up 425 + 68 in columns, which column does the 8 sit under?
options: Under the 5 in the Units (ones) column on the right
Under the 4 in the Hundreds column
Under the 2 in the Tens column
checks.why: Line up right-hand Units under Units (8 under 5) and Tens under Tens (6 under 2) before adding.

checks.question: In 342 − 127, we cannot do 2 − 7 without going negative. What is the right step?
options: Write 7 − 2 = 5
Borrow 1 ten from the 4 (leaving 3 tens) so the units become 12, then do 12 − 7 = 5
checks.why: Never subtract bottom-from-top! Borrow 1 ten from the next left column so top − bottom works cleanly.

checks.question: You worked out 342 − 127 = 215. How do you check it using addition?
options: 215 + 127 = 342 (matches the starting number!)
checks.why: Adding your answer back to what you subtracted returns the exact starting amount (215 + 127 = 342).

e3-multiplication-and-division.title: E3 Maths: Multiplication & Division with Remainders
e3-multiplication-and-division.subject: maths

checks.question: To multiply 34 × 6 without a calculator, how does splitting Tens & Units help?
options: Split 34 into 30 and 4: calculate (30 × 6 = 180) + (4 × 6 = 24) = 204
Multiply 3 × 6 + 4 = 22
Multiply 34 + 6 = 40
checks.why: Splitting 2-digit numbers into Tens and Units keeps mental multiplication simple and exact.

checks.question: When dividing 53 ÷ 4 = 13 remainder 1, how does the '13 r 1' translate to packing boxes of 4?
options: 13 full boxes with 1 item left over
13.1 items
4 boxes left over
checks.why: The quotient (13) tells how many full groups fit; the remainder (1) is the leftover items.

checks.question: 25 people need taxis that hold 4 passengers each (25 ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 1). How many taxis must you book?
options: 6 taxis
7 taxis (otherwise 1 person is stranded!)
5 taxis
checks.why: Always check the real-life situation: 6 taxis only seat 24, so you round UP to 7 taxis for everyone.

checks.question: When rounding 365 to the nearest 100, which digit decides whether it goes to 300 or 400?
options: The Tens digit (6) — since 6 is 5 or more, round UP to 400
The Units digit (5)
The Hundreds digit (3)
checks.why: Always look one column to the RIGHT of the place you are rounding to (Tens digit decides nearest 100; Units digit decides nearest 10).

checks.question: To estimate a £2.85 coffee + £4.10 sandwich + £1.95 cake quickly, what should you round each price to first?
options: Multiply all three numbers
Round to the nearest £100
checks.why: Rounding everyday prices to the nearest £1 (or 10p) lets you estimate totals in seconds and spot till or calculator mistakes.

checks.question: What does 297 round to when rounded to the nearest 10?
options: 300 (the 7 pushes 29 tens up to 30 tens = 300)
checks.why: 297 lies between 290 and 300 — because the units digit is 7 (5 or more), it rounds up to 300.

checks.question: In the fraction 3/4, what does the bottom number (4) tell you?
options: How many equal parts the whole is split into (4 equal quarters)
How many shaded pieces there are
That 3 is bigger than 4
checks.why: The denominator (bottom) tells the total equal parts in 1 whole; the numerator (top) counts how many of those parts you take.

checks.question: How do you work out 3/4 of £24 in two clear steps?
options: Divide £24 by 4 (= £6 for 1/4), then multiply £6 × 3 = £18
Divide £24 by 3 (= £8)
Multiply £24 × 4
checks.why: Find 1 quarter first (÷ 4 = £6), then take 3 of them (× 3 = £18).

checks.question: Which is larger: 1/4 of a pizza or 1/10 of the same pizza?
options: 1/4 is larger — splitting into 4 pieces makes bigger slices than splitting into 10 pieces
1/10 is larger because 10 is bigger than 4
They are equal
checks.why: For unit fractions (top = 1), a BIGGER bottom number means MORE shares and therefore a SMALLER slice!

e3-money-and-decimals.title: E3 Maths: Money, Change & Decimal Basics
e3-money-and-decimals.subject: maths

checks.question: How do you write '£4 and 5 pence' correctly in decimal pounds?
options: £4.05 (the 5 sits in the hundredths/single pence column)
checks.why: £4.50 is £4 and 50 pence; 5 pence is 5/100 of a pound, so write £4.05 with the 0 in the 10p column.

checks.question: You pay for a £6.75 book with a £10 note. What gives the right change cleanly?
options: Write £4.25 without borrowing
checks.why: Counting up to the next pound first (+25p to £7, +£3 to £10 = £3.25) avoids tricky zero-borrowing mistakes.

checks.question: Can you ever write an answer as '£3.40p' using BOTH £ and p together?
options: No — choose ONE unit only: either £3.40 or 340p
Yes — writing both earns bonus marks
Write £3.4
checks.why: Never mix £ and p on the same number (like £3.40p), and always write 2 decimal places when using £.

e3-time-clocks-and-calendars.title: E3 Maths: Telling the Time, Clocks & Calendars
e3-time-clocks-and-calendars.subject: maths

checks.question: What does '2:45 pm' look like on a 24-hour digital clock?
options: 14:45 (add 12 to the hour for afternoon/evening pm times)
checks.why: For 1:00 pm onwards, add 12 to the hours: 2 + 12 = 14 → 14:45.

checks.question: A film starts at 11:40 and lasts 1 hour 35 minutes. What time does it finish?
checks.why: Add whole hours first (12:40), bridge to the next hour (+20 mins → 13:00), then add the leftover 15 minutes (13:15).

checks.question: Remembering '30 days hath September, April, June, and November' — how many days are in a standard week and in July?
options: 7 days in a week; 31 days in July
5 days in a week; 30 days in July
7 days in a week; 28 days in July
checks.why: Counting weeks across month boundaries relies on knowing which months have 30 days vs 31 days (and 28/29 in February).

e3-everyday-measures-and-scales.title: E3 Maths: Length, Weight, Capacity & Reading Scales
e3-everyday-measures-and-scales.subject: maths

checks.question: Which everyday metric unit is best for measuring a bottle of juice vs a parcel's weight?
options: Juice capacity in millilitres (ml) or litres (l); parcel weight in grams (g) or kilograms (kg)
Both in centimetres (cm)
Juice in kilograms; parcel in litres
checks.why: Length = mm/cm/m/km; Mass/weight = g/kg; Liquid capacity = ml/l; Temperature = °C.

checks.question: A measuring jug shows marks at 200 ml and 400 ml with ONE unlabelled mark exactly halfway between them. What is that mark?
options: 300 ml (halfway between 200 and 400)
250 ml
201 ml
checks.why: Count the gaps between known labels: (400 − 200) ÷ 2 gaps = 100 ml per step, so the middle mark reads 300 ml.

checks.question: Before writing your final measurement on an Entry 3 exam answer line, what must you always check?
options: Include the unit (cm, kg, ml, °C) and confirm the scale steps weren't counted by 1s when each gap equals 2, 5, or 10
Leave units blank
Always read the number above the pointer
checks.why: Checking both the gap size and writing the right unit secures full measurement marks.

e3-shapes-angles-and-directions.title: E3 Maths: Shapes, Right Angles & Directions
e3-shapes-angles-and-directions.subject: maths

checks.question: How many degrees are in a Right Angle (corner of a square or book)?
options: 90° (a quarter turn)
180° (a half turn)
checks.why: A right angle is 90° (one quarter of a full 360° circle) and can be tested easily against the square corner of a ruler or paper.

checks.question: You face NORTH and turn ONE quarter turn CLOCKWISE. Which compass direction do you face now?
options: East (Never Eat Shredded Wheat clockwise: N → E → S → W)
West
South
checks.why: Clockwise around the compass goes N → E → S → W; anti-clockwise goes N → W → S → E.

checks.question: Which shape is a 3D solid (like a tin of soup) rather than a flat 2D shape?
options: Cylinder (3D) — whereas circle, square, and pentagon are flat 2D shapes
Circle
Rectangle
checks.why: 2D shapes are flat (circle, triangle, rectangle, hexagon); 3D solids have depth (cube, cuboid, cylinder, sphere, pyramid).

e3-lists-tallies-tables-and-charts.title: E3 Maths: Lists, Tally Charts, Tables & Bar Charts
e3-lists-tallies-tables-and-charts.subject: maths

checks.question: In a tally chart, what total does two crossed 5-gates plus 3 single lines represent?
checks.why: Each crossed gate stands for 5, making counting large surveys fast and clean: 5 + 5 + 3 = 13.

checks.question: When reading a two-way table for 'Tuesday Morning', how do you find the exact cell?
options: Trace across the Tuesday row and down the Morning column to where they meet
Add the whole Tuesday row together
Read the top-left corner
checks.why: Match both row label and column header with your finger or ruler so you never slip onto the row above or below.

checks.question: On a vertical bar chart axis marked 0, 5, 10, 15, a bar stops halfway between 10 and 15. Wait — why check if half-steps make sense, or if axis steps are 2s?
options: Always read the exact vertical axis scale (whether steps go up in 1s, 2s, 5s, or 10s) and label both axes when drawing your own
Always guess 12
Ignore axis numbers and measure bar colour
checks.why: Reading the axis step size first and ensuring uniform numbered scales when drawing bars avoids the #1 E3 chart slip.

e3-english-reading-everyday-texts.title: E3 English: Reading Signs, Emails & Instructions
e3-english-reading-everyday-texts.subject: english

checks.question: A notice says 'Library Closed Tuesday for Flooring Works — Return Books via Drop Box'. What is its main purpose?
options: To inform readers of the closure and tell them how to return books
To entertain readers with a fictional story
To sell library furniture
checks.why: Everyday signs, emails, and notices usually aim to inform, instruct, warn, or invite action.

checks.question: When a question asks for a specific opening time or postcode from a flyer, what finds it fastest?
options: Scan headings, bullet lists, and numbers rather than re-reading every word slowly
Guess based on your local library
Copy the whole opening paragraph
checks.why: Headings, bold labels, and numbers act as signposts guiding your eye straight to the requested fact.

checks.question: If the question asks 'Give TWO items visitors must bring', what happens if you write three details from memory instead of the text?
options: Only details clearly stated in the provided text earn marks — outside guesses score zero
Anything sensible always earns full marks
Writing only one item still gives full marks
checks.why: Always check the exact count asked for ('give TWO') and lift the facts strictly from the source text.

e3-english-sentence-basics.title: E3 English: Capitals, Full Stops & Joining Words
e3-english-sentence-basics.subject: english

checks.question: Which group ALWAYS needs a capital letter in English sentences?
options: Every first word of a sentence, the pronoun 'I', and proper nouns (people, towns, days, months)
Every food item and colour
Only the title at the top of the page
checks.why: Remember MINTS: Months, I, Names (people & places), Titles, and Start of sentences always take a capital letter.

checks.question: Which joining word correctly connects a contrast: 'I arrived on time, [ ? ] the doors were locked'?
options: but
because
so
checks.why: 'and' adds similar points, 'but' shows a contrast, 'because' gives a reason, and 'so' shows a result.

checks.question: Which sentence uses 'was' or 'were' accurately?
options: 'We was late to the workshop.'
'We were early, and the hall was ready.'
'They was very helpful.'
checks.why: Use 'was' for one person/thing (I/he/she/the hall was); use 'were' for plural groups and 'you' (we/they/you were).

e3-english-everyday-spellings.title: E3 English: Everyday Spellings, Plurals & Homophones
e3-english-everyday-spellings.subject: english

checks.question: What is the correct plural of 'box', 'bus', and 'city'?
options: boxes, buses, cities
boxs, buss, citys
boxies, buses, cityes
checks.why: Words ending in -x, -s, -sh, -ch add -es; words ending in consonant + y swap -y for -ies (city → cities).

checks.question: Choose the right words: 'Please [ ? ] for the bus [ ? ] the entrance.'
options: wait / by
weight / buy
wait / buy
checks.why: 'wait' = stay in expectation (vs weight = heaviness); 'by' = beside/near (vs buy = purchase).

checks.question: Which everyday words all keep their silent letters spelled cleanly?
options: Wednesday, February, know, write
Wensday, Febuary, now, rite
Wedensday, Febry, kno, wright
checks.why: Sound out tricky letters slowly when spelling ('Wed-nes-day', 'Feb-ru-ary', silent 'k' in know, silent 'w' in write).

e3-english-writing-emails-and-forms.title: E3 English: Writing Short Emails, Notes & Forms
e3-english-writing-emails-and-forms.subject: english

checks.question: Before writing a short email or filling in an application form, what should you check in 30 seconds?
options: Who you are writing to, why you are writing, and every bullet point you must include
How many long uncommon words you can squeeze in
Whether you can skip dates and names
checks.why: Listing 1 keyword per required bullet keeps your short message focused and prevents missing required facts.

checks.question: What four simple parts structure a polite Entry 3 email cleanly?
options: 1) Clear Subject line, 2) Polite greeting ('Dear...'), 3) Short clear paragraphs covering every point, 4) Polite sign-off + full name
Just one unpunctuated sentence with no greeting or name
A comic title and emoji sign-off
checks.why: Even short Entry 3 emails earn format marks from a clear Subject, greeting, organised points, and polite closing.

checks.question: When a form specifies 'Use BLOCK CAPITALS' or 'Format DD/MM/YYYY', what loses easy marks?
options: Writing in lowercase cursive or mixing up month and day format (MM/DD/YY)
Writing your postcode clearly in capitals
Checking every box is answered or marked N/A
checks.why: Forms test following exact instructions — follow BLOCK CAPITALS, tick-boxes, and UK DD/MM/YYYY date formats strictly.
